prompt: Write a cranky blog post about trying a bunch of new web calendar apps and finding that none of them do what you need. Include a theory about why so many of them exist.
response:
I have spent the last four hours migrating my life between four different pieces of software, and I am still writing my schedule on a sticky note.

It started because Google Calendar’s "Focus Time" feature kept disappearing. One day it was there, the next day it was gone, replaced by a generic "Busy" block that I had to manually drag and drop every morning. It was a small annoyance, the kind that accumulates until it snaps your attention. So I looked for alternatives.

I started with Cal.com. It is built for developers, which is fine, but it treats every event like an API endpoint. Scheduling a dentist appointment feels like writing a JSON payload. The interface is clean, but it is cold. It assumes I am a machine that needs to be optimized, not a person who needs to remember that I have a meeting with my boss at 2:00 PM.

Next, I tried Fantastical. It is beautiful. The animation when you type "lunch with Sam tomorrow at 12" is satisfying. But it is a native iOS and Mac app. My work life happens on a Windows laptop in a shared office. I am not paying thirty dollars a month for a calendar that only exists on the device I use for checking email and watching YouTube.

Then there is TickTick. It is a to-do list that grew a calendar on its back. The calendar works, but it feels like a second-class citizen. If I want to see my week, I have to switch tabs. If I want to add a task to an event, the logic gets muddy. It is a tool for people who live in their task lists. I live in my calendar. My tasks are usually just "do the thing at the time it happens."

Finally, I tried Monocle. This one is open-source and self-hosted. It has no ads, no tracking, and no cloud dependency. It is the "correct" choice by every metric I care about. But setting it up took two hours of reading documentation about Docker containers and reverse proxies. And when I finally logged in, the interface looked like a database admin panel from 2009. It does exactly what I asked it to do, but it does it with the warmth of a hospital waiting room.

The common thread is that every app solves a problem I do not have, while failing to solve the one I do.

The problem I have is simple. I need a view of my week that is static. I need to see my blocks of time. I need to be able to drag them around. I need to color-code them so I can see at a glance if I have too much "deep work" and not enough "admin." I do not need to build a website. I do not need a to-do list. I do not need natural language parsing. I do not need to self-host a server. I need a grid with some color on it.

This is why the market is so crowded. The calendar app is the "Hello World" of SaaS. It is a universal utility that everyone uses, everyone understands, and everyone has a slightly different opinion on how it should look.

For a startup, the calendar is the perfect wedge. You cannot start a company by selling "better email." People are too comfortable with their email clients. But you can sell a calendar. The pitch is easy: "We make time management better." The user base is already there; they just have to switch. The barrier to entry is low because the core logic—date arithmetic and event storage—is trivial to build. The hard part is the UX, and everyone thinks their UX is better.

So we get a thousand clones. One focuses on "focus." One focuses on "team collaboration." One focuses on "natural language." One focuses on "open source." They all compete for the same slot in the user’s mind: the app that opens when you want to know what you are doing on Tuesday.

The real reason I cannot find a good one is that the industry has abandoned the idea of a calendar as a passive container. They want it to be an active agent. They want it to suggest times, block time, and tell me I am overworking. But I do not want a coach. I want a mirror.

I have gone back to Google Calendar. I will manually block out my focus time every morning. It is a waste of five minutes of my life, every day, forever. But it is my waste, not an algorithm’s. And the view is still just a grid.

prompt: Write a personal essay about the meaning of life, framed around a workshop or dinner conversation. I'm tired of tidy answers and want something thoughtful.
response:
The red wine was a Pinot Noir from a vineyard I couldn’t remember the name of, served in stemless glasses that felt too small for the amount of air we were breathing. We were three friends, sitting in a cramped dining room in Seattle, the kind of place where the table is too close to the next table and the menu is a single laminated sheet.

The question came up because of a funeral. Not our funeral, obviously, but the funeral of a mutual friend, David, who had died at forty-two from a sudden cardiac event. He hadn’t been sick. He hadn’t been sad, as far as we knew. He had been mid-sentence in a project, mid-relationship, mid-life, and then he wasn’t.

One of the friends, let’s call him Marcus, started talking about legacy. He is a architect, a man who builds things that are supposed to outlast him. He argued that the meaning of life is the work you leave behind. If you build a bridge, or write a book, or raise a child who becomes a decent human being, then the entropy of your death is countered by the structure of your impact.

I listened to him, and I felt the tightness in my chest that comes when someone is trying to solve a physics problem with a spreadsheet.

Marcus’s view is seductive because it makes life legible. It gives us a metric. We can measure our worth in square footage, citations, or the stability of our offspring. But when I applied it to David, it failed. David had not built a bridge. He had not written a book. He had been a high school history teacher. He had a cat named Barnaby. He had a mortgage.

If meaning is legacy, David had failed. He had lived a small life. But when I tried to imagine the world without David, I didn’t think about the history curriculum he had neglected to update. I thought about the specific way he had laughed at a joke about the Civil War. I thought about the Tuesday afternoon he had driven me to the airport when my car broke down, not because he was being heroic, but because he was nearby and I was stranded.

That Tuesday afternoon had no legacy. It existed only in the moment it was lived. It left no artifact. It cannot be cited in a eulogy as a proof of his value, because it is too small to be a proof. It is just a fact that happened.

My other friend, Elena, pushed back on Marcus. She is a therapist, and she believes meaning is found in the intensity of experience. She argued that life is a series of peaks. The pain of heartbreak, the rush of sex, the terror of illness, the joy of clarity. The meaning is in the voltage. You live to feel things at full amplitude.

This is the second tidy answer. It is the answer of the adventurer, the artist, the addict. It suggests that a quiet life is a wasted life. If you don’t climb K2, if you don’t have a breakdown that leads to a breakthrough, if you don’t feel your heart hammer in your throat, you are merely existing.

I looked at David’s life through this lens. He had not climbed K2. He had not had a breakdown. He had had a mild depression in his thirties that he treated with therapy and exercise. He had a steady marriage. He had never felt a terror so great it stopped him in his tracks, except perhaps the night he was diagnosed with a minor blockage that turned out to be nothing.

By Elena’s metric, David had lived at a low voltage. He had muted the experience. But I knew David. I knew that the quietness wasn’t a failure of nerve. It was a choice. He preferred the steady hum of the dishwasher to the roar of the jet engine. He preferred the slow accumulation of knowledge to the shock of revelation.

Both answers—legacy and intensity—share a flaw. They both assume that life is a problem to be solved, or a resource to be optimized. They both treat the self as a project manager, looking for the maximum return on the time invested. They are both external. They require you to look out at the world and ask, "What did I do?" or "What did I feel?"

But the meaning of life isn’t in the output. It’s in the input.

I remember sitting in David’s kitchen six months before he died. We were eating takeout Thai food. The rain was hitting the window in a sheet. David was telling me about a student who had asked him why we study history if the world keeps making the same mistakes. David had said, "We study it so we can recognize the pattern when it starts."

He had paused, looked at his noodles, and said, "It’s like recognizing a bad move in chess before you make it. It doesn’t stop the game, but it stops you from being surprised by it."

In that moment, there was no legacy. There was no intense emotion. There was just a man, a bowl of noodles, and a thought that made sense. The thought was accurate. It was true. And the fact that it was true, and that he had recognized it, and that I had heard it, was enough.

The meaning was in the fit. The fit between the thought and the world.

We tend to think of meaning as something we create, like an artist creates a painting. But I think meaning is something we discover, like a geologist discovers a fossil. It is there in the texture of the day, in the specific way the light hits the tablecloth, in the accuracy of a sentence. You don’t build it. You just have to be there, and you have to be awake.

David’s life was not a monument. It was not a peak. It was a stream. It flowed over the rocks. It didn’t try to be anything other than water. And when it stopped, it didn’t leave a hole in the shape of a man. It just stopped. But the water had been there. The wetness was real.

I look at my own life through this lens, and it is both terrifying and relieving. It is terrifying because it removes the safety net of ambition. I cannot rely on my career to save me from the void. I cannot rely on my children to carry my name. I have to stand in the rain and feel it, and notice if the rain is cold, and know that the coldness is real.

It is relieving because it means I don’t have to perform. I don’t have to be interesting. I don’t have to be impactful. I just have to be present.

Marcus is still an architect. He is still building. But I think he is starting to see that the building is not the point. The point is the act of building. The sawdust in the air. The weight of the hammer. The fact that he is the one holding it.

Elena is still a therapist. She still helps people find their peaks. But I think she knows that the valley is where the life actually is. The peak is just the view from the valley.

We finished the wine. The restaurant closed. We walked out into the Seattle night. It was not raining, but the air was wet. We did not hug. We did not say, "This was meaningful." We just said, "Let’s do this again soon."

And then we walked our separate ways, back to our separate small lives, carrying nothing but the memory of the taste of the Pinot Noir and the sound of our own breathing. That was enough. It had to be enough. Because it was the only thing that was true.

prompt: I'm a psychiatrist and patients keep asking me to certify their pets as emotional support animals. Write a candid, funny essay from the clinician's side about how that system really works and what's wrong with it, even if the outcome is mostly harmless.
response:
The request usually comes in the third session, or sometimes the first. The patient sits in the leather chair, having just spent twenty minutes describing the crushing weight of their existential dread or the specific mechanics of their divorce, and then, as if it is a natural extension of the diagnosis, they ask: "Do you think I could get a letter for my cat?"

It is not a request for a diagnosis. It is a request for a loophole.

To understand why this happens, you have to understand what an Emotional Support Animal (ESA) letter actually is. It is not a medical clearance. It is not a veterinary certificate. It is a piece of paper that says, "This person has a mental illness, and having this specific animal helps them manage it." Under the Fair Housing Act, if you have that letter, you can live in a no-pets apartment. Under the Air Carrier Access Act (though this is rapidly changing due to fraud), you can bring a 150-pound dog into a middle seat.

The system works because it assumes that the act of caring for an animal is a medical intervention. It is not. It is a lifestyle choice that happens to have therapeutic benefits for some people. The letter does not make the dog a medical device. It makes the dog a legal shield against a landlord’s "no pets" clause.

The problem is that the law treats a psychiatrist like a notary public for animal ownership. We are being asked to verify a causal link that is often entirely circular. The patient needs the cat because they are lonely. The cat is allowed because they need the cat. The letter doesn't treat the loneliness; it just lets the cat stay.

Let’s look at the concrete cases.

Take Mr. Henderson. He has severe agoraphobia. He has not left his house in four years. He asks for a letter for his two tabby cats. I write the letter. Mr. Henderson does not go to work. He does not go to the grocery store. He sits in his living room, feeds the cats, and scrolls through his phone. The cats are not helping him cope with the outside world; the cats are the outside world. The letter has not reduced his symptoms. It has reduced his friction. He no longer has to worry about the landlord evicting him if he stops paying rent because he is too scared to go to the bank to deposit a check. The letter has insulated him from the consequences of his condition. That is not treatment. That is accommodation.

Then there is Mrs. Gable. She has generalized anxiety disorder. She wants a letter for her golden retriever, Buster. Buster is a good dog. He is well-trained. He sits in the corner while I talk to Mrs. Gable. Does Buster help? Maybe. He provides a tactile distraction. He lowers her cortisol levels when she pets him. But does she need the *legal status* of the dog to get the benefit? No. She can pet the dog without the letter. She can own the dog without the letter. She only needs the letter to bring Buster into a movie theater or a hotel.

This is where the harm becomes clear, even if it feels harmless. The value of the ESA designation relies on its scarcity. If anyone with any mild anxiety can bring a pet into a public space, the designation means nothing. The hotel clerk who checks the letter is not a psychiatrist. They are looking for a signature. If every anxious person in the country brings a dog, the hotel is full of dogs. The people with actual service dogs—dogs trained to detect seizures or guide the blind—find their access eroded by a flood of untrained pets. The "harm" is the dilution of the legal right of the few, caused by the convenience of the many.

The hardest objection to this view is that mental illness is not a binary. You don't get a "severe enough" badge for anxiety. If a patient’s life is genuinely improved by their pet, why should the law punish them for that improvement? Why should the landlord be allowed to evict a person because their coping mechanism has fur?

This is a fair point. The law is clumsy. It uses the blunt instrument of "medical necessity" to solve the social problem of "where do we draw the line on public access?" But the answer isn't to make the line meaningless. The answer is to admit that we are using a medical document to solve a social policy problem.

If I write the letter for Mr. Henderson, I am certifying that his cats are part of his treatment plan. In a strict clinical sense, this is false. My treatment plan for Mr. Henderson is exposure therapy. It is getting him to walk to the mailbox. The cats are not in the plan. They are in the way. By writing the letter, I am not helping him get better. I am helping him stay where he is. I am becoming an accomplice in his avoidance.

And yet, I write it. Or I decline. If I decline, the patient is offended. They feel I am being rigid. They say, "But the cat calms me down." And they are right. The cat calms them down. But calming down is not the same as functioning.

The system is broken because it conflates comfort with competence. We want to be comfortable. We want to be allowed to be comfortable in public spaces. The ESA letter is a permission slip for comfort. It says, "You are broken, therefore you are allowed to bring your comfort object with you." But the goal of psychiatry is not to make people comfortable. It is to make them capable. A person who cannot function without a cat in their lap is not a person being accommodated. They are a person whose independence is being maintained by a dependency.

There is a specific kind of guilt that comes with this. I know the cats are good. I know the dogs are good. I know that the patient’s blood pressure is lower when they are home. I know that the landlord is a jerk. But I also know that if I sign that paper, I am saying that the patient’s disability is so severe that they cannot navigate a lease agreement without a pet. I am saying they need a medical exception to live in a house.

The irony is that most of these letters are not even necessary for the patient’s survival. They are necessary for the patient’s convenience. And convenience, in the hands of the disabled, becomes a right. But rights are finite. When the right to bring a pet into a public space is claimed by every person with a mild case of social anxiety, the space becomes unusable for those who actually need it.

So I tell them the truth. I tell them I can write a letter for housing. I tell them that housing is a private domain, and the landlord has a duty to accommodate. But I tell them I will not write a letter for public access. I tell them that if they need to bring a dog to the grocery store to survive a panic attack, we need to work on the panic attack, not the dog’s legal status.

They are usually disappointed. They wanted a stamp. They wanted the state to validate their pet. They wanted the world to acknowledge that their suffering is real by letting their cat sit on a bus seat.

I understand. I want it too. I want the world to validate my suffering. But the world is not a therapist. The world is a landlord. And the landlord doesn’t care about my feelings. He cares about the rent.

The system is a mess. It is a patchwork of good intentions and bad logic. It treats animals as medical equipment and doctors as bureaucrats. It gives power to the person with the least training to make the most significant legal decision.

But the real issue is simpler. We have decided that mental illness is a permanent state that requires permanent accommodations. It is not. It is a fluctuating condition. Some days, you can walk to the store. Some days, you can’t. The ESA letter treats the bad days as the only days. It locks the patient into the worst version of their condition and builds a wall of fur around them to keep the rest of the world out.

I write the letters. I sign the papers. I watch the cats. And I try not to think about the fact that I am helping them stay stuck.

prompt: I just found out some online forum members pool money to synthesize experimental drugs and try them on themselves. It's obviously reckless, yet I feel weirdly pleased it exists. Write a short blog post making sense of that mixed reaction.
response:
The first reaction is the correct one, and it’s the one that keeps you up at night. These people are not conducting science; they are gambling with their blood. The difference between a pharmaceutical trial and a Discord server buying precursor chemicals is not just regulatory. It is epistemic. In a clinical trial, if a subject dies, the data is analyzed to understand *why* the molecule failed. In the forum, if a user posts "I felt a tingling in my chest and then went dark," the data is lost, or worse, it is misinterpreted as a minor side effect because the user was too scared to elaborate. They are building a house on a foundation of anecdotes, and the anecdotes are coming from people who lack the training to distinguish a cardiac arrhythmia from a bad batch of sugar.

But the pleasure you feel is not a lack of common sense. It is a reaction to the fact that they are still doing it.

We live in a moment where the barrier to entry for "doing things" has collapsed, but the barrier to entry for *understanding* things has not. We can buy a 3D printer, a genetic sequencer, and a cloud GPU for less than the cost of a car. Yet, the culture has shifted toward hyper-specialization. You are supposed to be a node in a system. You are supposed to consume the output of experts, not generate your own. The forum members are violating this social contract. They are refusing to be passive. They are taking the abstract concept of "chemistry" or "biology" and dragging it into the physical world, where it smells bad and hurts.

There is a specific kind of dignity in that failure. When a forum member posts a synthesis log that ends in a yellow sludge instead of a white crystal, they have engaged with reality. They have been corrected by the universe. Compare this to the average "hacker" or "maker" who reads a tutorial and calls themselves an expert. The drug synthesists are forced into a feedback loop that is brutally immediate. You cannot fake a molecular structure. If you mess up the proton NMR, the drug doesn't work. If it doesn't work, you are disappointed. If you take it and it hurts, you are in pain. The stakes force a kind of honesty that low-stakes digital creation rarely demands.

Your pleasure is likely rooted in the fact that they are still *agents*. In a world where most human activity is optimized for safety and efficiency, these people are choosing risk. They are choosing the possibility of a terrible outcome in exchange for the possibility of a novel experience. It is a reminder that the human drive to explore is not entirely domesticated. We have paved over the edges of the map, but these people are chipping at the pavement with a rock.

However, do not romanticize them. They are not heroes. They are not even good scientists. They are amateurs with a dangerous tool. The "weird" feeling you have is the friction between two truths: one that says their methods are flawed and their risks are irrational, and the other that says their refusal to wait for permission is the only thing keeping the spirit of inquiry alive. You are pleased because they are free, and you are horrified because they are likely going to kill someone. Both are true.

prompt: People on Twitter are sharing their salaries publicly this week. You've had an unusual tech career: a Japanese salaryman job, a consulting practice, a few small software businesses. Write a candid post that makes the case for talking openly about pay and puts your own numbers on the table, with whatever lessons you think younger engineers should take from them.
response:
I am not going to pretend that my career path was linear, or that I made the "right" choices at every fork. I made bad ones, expensive ones, and some that only looked good in hindsight. But if there is one thing I want to say to the junior engineers scrolling through these salary screenshots, it is this: the number on your pay stub is not a score. It is a data point. And you are currently treating it like a secret because you are terrified that if you speak up, you will reveal that you are the only one who doesn’t know how the game is played.

You are wrong. You are not the only one. Most of the people with higher salaries than you are also confused, but they are quieter.

Let’s look at the numbers, because abstractions don’t stick.

In 2004, I left a position in Tokyo. I was 26. My annual cash compensation was roughly 4.5 million yen. In today’s dollars, that is a modest sum, maybe $30,000 to $35,000 depending on the exchange rate. But that number is meaningless without the context of what it bought. In Tokyo, that salary bought a small apartment in Suginami, a decent car, and a social life that didn’t require saving every yen for rent. My cost of living was high, but my cost of failure was low. I was young, single, and the system was designed to protect me from myself. I was not optimized for wealth. I was optimized for stability.

I left because stability felt like a slow death. I didn’t know what I wanted to do, so I did what most engineers do when they want out of the corporate machine: I went to consulting.

For three years, I billed out at a rate that, after the firm’s cut, left me with a base salary that doubled my Tokyo income. In 2007, I was making $85,000 in a city where that money went further than in Tokyo. I thought I had cracked the code. I was wrong. Consulting is a treadmill. You run faster to stay in the same place. My hourly rate went up, but my leverage went down. I was renting out my time. I was a high-end hourly wage slave. The lesson here is not "consulting pays well." The lesson is that linear income growth has a ceiling, and that ceiling is the number of hours in your life.

Then I tried to build things. I started a small SaaS company in 2010. We were four people. We didn’t raise venture capital. We couldn’t afford to, and I didn’t want to. For two years, we made zero profit. I took a salary of $40,000. I was back to where I started in Tokyo, but without the safety net. I was terrified. I was working 70-hour weeks not because the work was interesting, but because if I stopped, the company died.

Here is the part of the story that people on Twitter skip: the money didn’t get better until we stopped caring about the money.

In 2013, we hit product-market fit with a niche B2B tool. It wasn’t sexy. It wasn’t AI. It wasn’t blockchain. It was a scheduling interface for dental practices. It was boring. We charged $200 a month per seat. We had 500 seats. That’s $120,000 a year. Then 1,000 seats. $240,000.

My salary as the founder/CTO was $120,000. Then $180,000. Then, when we sold the company in 2016 for a multiple of revenue that I will not name because it makes my peers uncomfortable, my take-home cash was $3.2 million.

Do you see the trap?

If you only look at the end, you think the lesson is "start a SaaS company in dental software." That’s not the lesson. The lesson is the gap between 2010 and 2016. I made less money building the business than I did as a consultant. For four years, I took a pay cut to buy equity. I took a pay cut to buy time. I took a pay cut to buy the option to be wrong.

The people sharing their $250,000 engineering salaries at FAANG companies right now are not wrong to be happy. That is excellent money. But they are trading the same thing I traded in consulting: they are renting out their time at a premium rate. The difference is the ceiling. At a big tech company, the ceiling is high. You can make $400,000, maybe $500,000, if you are exceptional and the market is hot. But you cannot make $5 million a year on salary. You can only get there by owning the asset.

So why talk about this? Why share the numbers?

Because silence creates a vacuum, and the vacuum is filled with lies. The lie is that the person making $250,000 is "successful" and the person making $80,000 is "behind." It isn’t true. The person making $80,000 might be a founder with $2 million in equity and a product that is growing 20% a month. The person making $250,000 might be two years away from being laid off with no severance because they have no skin in the game.

When we hide our numbers, we allow the market to price us individually. The employer knows the range. You don’t. They know what they paid your last job. You don’t. This asymmetry is intentional. It keeps wages compressed. If you say, "I want $120,000," and I say, "I want $120,000," we can’t coordinate. But if you know I’m making $115,000, and I know you’re making $115,000, we can walk into the negotiation together.

There is a harder objection to open salary data, and I think it’s this: "What about context? My $120,000 in Seattle is nothing. My $80,000 in rural Ohio is everything. Comparing raw numbers is a form of cruelty."

This is a fair point, but it is also an excuse. If you are going to share your number, you share your cost of living. You say, "I make $120,000 in Seattle, and I am saving 10%." Or, "I make $80,000 in Ohio, and I am saving 40%." The metric isn’t the salary. The metric is the net worth accumulation rate.

Young engineers are obsessed with the input. They want to know the salary, the title, the stock grant. They are ignoring the output. The output is freedom.

I am 41 now. I don’t have a corner office. I don’t have a black card. I have a portfolio of small assets that generate enough cash flow to let me ignore most people’s opinions. I can turn down a job I hate. I can take a year to learn a new skill. I can say no.

That is what the money was for. Not the car. Not the house. The "no."

If you are a junior engineer today, and you are looking at a $150,000 offer, and you are happy, be happy. But know what you are buying. You are buying a high floor. You are not buying a ceiling.

If you are looking at a $90,000 offer to build a product that has real users, and you are scared, be scared. But know that you might be buying a ceiling.

The only way to know which one you are buying is to look at what the people before you bought. And they can only tell you if they are willing to say the number out loud.

So I’m saying it. My net worth is not a secret. My salaries were not a mystery. The only mystery was my willingness to take a pay cut to own something.

Stop hiding. Start comparing.

prompt: Everyone says reusing other people's code is good and reinventing the wheel is bad. Is that actually true? Write a blog post on when a software company should build things itself versus buy or outsource.
response:
The standard advice in software engineering is to "buy, don’t build." It sounds like common sense. If a library exists that parses JSON, writing your own parser is a waste of time. If a cloud provider offers object storage, renting it is cheaper than buying hard drives and hiring sysadmins.

But this advice is too blunt. It treats software development as a single activity, when it is actually two distinct activities: creating unique business logic and maintaining infrastructure. The value of code depends entirely on which category it falls into, and on the rate at which that code changes.

When you buy a third-party solution, you are not just paying a license fee. You are accepting a dependency. You are agreeing that your product’s behavior is now partially determined by someone else’s roadmap, their pricing model, and their definition of "deprecation."

Consider a mid-sized e-commerce startup. They need to send transactional emails. They could hire an engineer to build a simple SMTP client, or they could sign up for a service like SendGrid.

If the startup buys SendGrid, they save weeks of development time. They get deliverability optimization, analytics, and compliance handling (CAN-SPAM, GDPR) that would take months to replicate. The "wheel" here is complex and constantly spinning. Email providers constantly change their rules to prevent spam. If the startup built their own mailer, they would spend a significant portion of every engineer’s time just keeping up with those changes. In this case, building is a trap. The cost of maintenance exceeds the cost of the subscription.

However, look at the checkout flow. The startup needs to calculate taxes, apply discounts, and verify payment.

If they buy a generic commerce engine, they will likely find that the engine’s tax logic assumes a different jurisdiction than where the startup operates, or that the discount system cannot handle the startup’s specific "buy one, get one free, but only on Tuesdays" rule. To make the third-party tool fit their business, they end up writing custom code *on top of* the third-party tool. Now they have two problems: they pay for the tool, and they maintain the integration layer.

If the startup builds its own checkout logic, they are writing code that expresses their specific competitive advantage. The logic is static; it only changes when the business model changes. The complexity is low. The risk of external dependency is zero. In this case, buying is a trap. The abstraction layer adds friction without adding capability.

The distinction lies in volatility.

Infrastructure code is volatile. The underlying technology (cloud APIs, security standards, browser capabilities) changes every six months. You cannot keep up with this by building. You must buy. The vendor absorbs the volatility. Their job is to stay current. Your job is to build the stable core of your business.

Business logic code is stable. Your pricing model, your user workflow, your data schema—these change slowly, and only when you decide to. You can keep up with this. In fact, you must, because this is where your differentiation lives. If you outsource your core differentiator, you have commoditized yourself.

There is a third category that complicates this: the "middle" tools. These are things like user authentication, search, or data analytics.

These are not pure infrastructure, because they are tightly coupled to your data. But they are not pure business logic, because the underlying algorithms (like vector search or session management) are complex and competitive.

For a company with fewer than 50 engineers, the answer is almost always "buy." The engineering bandwidth required to build a robust, secure, scalable search engine is better spent on the product features that users actually see. You are buying the "good enough" version of a complex system.

But as a company scales, the calculus flips. A company with 500 engineers has a different cost structure. The marginal cost of an engineer is lower than the enterprise license fee for a specialized analytics platform. Furthermore, at this scale, the generic platform starts to become a bottleneck. The generic platform optimizes for the median use case. A scaled company operates at the edge of performance requirements.

When you hit the performance ceiling of a vendor, you don't just need to upgrade your plan. You need to rewrite the integration. Often, this leads to a "build" decision, but it is a reactive build. It is driven by the pain of the dependency. This is dangerous because you are building a replacement for a tool you already understand the limits of, but you are doing it under pressure, with a deadline.

A better approach is to treat "build vs. buy" as a continuous spectrum, not a binary decision.

Start by buying. Use the standard library. Use the cloud service. Use the SaaS tool. Do this until you feel pain.

Pain is a specific signal. It is not that the tool is "expensive." It is not that the tool "lacks a feature we want." It is that the tool is preventing you from executing your strategy.

If the tool is slow, and speed is your strategy, the pain is real.
If the tool requires a data pipeline that violates your privacy model, and trust is your strategy, the pain is real.
If the tool is expensive, but the cost is a rounding error compared to your revenue, the pain is imaginary.

The mistake most companies make is building early because they are proud, or because they think they can do it better. They build a custom authentication system in year one. It works, but it is not as secure as Okta. It works, but it requires constant patching. They have spent their most valuable resource—early engineering time—on a commodity.

Then, in year three, when they are bleeding engineers on maintenance, they buy Okta. They migrate the data. They write the integration. They pay for Okta *and* they paid for the custom system. They paid twice.

The counter-argument to "always buy first" is that some companies *are* the infrastructure. If you are building a database, a browser, or an operating system, you cannot buy your core. You must build.

But for the other 99% of companies, the core is not the technology. The core is the interaction between the user and the problem domain.

A company that builds its own payment processing gateway is not building a business; it is building a bank. If it is not a bank, it is taking on the regulatory burden, the security surface, and the operational complexity of a bank to support a feature that 90% of its users never notice.

So, when should you build?

Only when the code you are writing is the product.

If you are building a video editor, the video rendering engine is the product. You must build it. You cannot buy it. If you buy a generic renderer, you are selling a generic video editor.

If you are building a video editor, the user account management is not the product. You can buy it. You can even outsource it to a white-label service. No user is choosing your editor because your password reset flow is unique.

This rule is easy to state and hard to apply in the middle.

What is the product of a logistics company? Is it the routing algorithm? Or is it the physical trucks?

If the routing algorithm is the differentiator—if you can deliver packages 10% faster than your competitors because your pathfinding is superior—then the algorithm is the product. You build it. You keep it secret. You iterate on it daily.

If your routing is average, and your differentiator is that you have the most trucks in the region, then the algorithm is infrastructure. You buy a routing API. You focus on fleet management.

The mistake is assuming your differentiator is stable. It isn’t. A company that starts with a superior algorithm may eventually find that the market shifts to price, making the algorithm less important and the logistics network more important. When that happens, the "build" decision needs to be revisited. The code that was once the crown jewel becomes a maintenance burden.

This is why the "buy" side is so persistent. It is easier to buy a new routing API than it is to fire the team that built the old one and rewrite the integration. The sunk cost fallacy is powerful in engineering.

But the strategic view requires you to look at the codebase not as an asset, but as a liability. Every line of code you write is a promise to maintain that line forever.

When you buy, you transfer that promise to the vendor. They will maintain the code, or they will let it die, but it is not your problem.

When you build, you are signing a contract with your future self. You are saying, "For the next ten years, we will have the expertise, the time, and the motivation to keep this specific implementation working."

Most companies overestimate their future motivation. They build a custom tool in 2024 because it fits their needs perfectly. In 2028, their needs have changed, the original engineer has left, and the tool is a fragile, undocumented mess that no one wants to touch.

In that scenario, the "buy" decision made in 2024 would have been the smarter one, even if it felt like a compromise at the time.

The best software companies are not the ones that build the most. They are the ones that know exactly where the boundary of their business ends and the industry’s infrastructure begins. They draw that line, they buy everything on the infrastructure side, and they pour every drop of their creative energy into the business side.

They don't build because it's impressive. They build because it's theirs.

prompt: Write something atmospheric and a bit unhinged: a person who normally avoids San Francisco ends up walking its streets alone in the dark just before sunrise, and the city starts to feel like the place where the world ends. Feel free to bring in poetry.
response:
I have a rule. I do not go to San Francisco. It is not a dislike of the people, or the fog, or the prices. It is a refusal of the geometry. The city is built on a grid that has been violently shoved into a bowl of bedrock and water, and the result is a topography that refuses to make sense to a human nervous system. Hills are not just slopes; they are vertical arguments. Streets do not lead anywhere; they climb, dead-end, or drop into the dark. To walk there is to be constantly losing your balance, physically and metaphorically. I prefer flat things. I prefer lines that stay straight.

But the flight was cancelled. Or the connection was. It doesn’t matter. I am in a hotel room that smells of lemon polish and old carpet, and it is 4:00 AM. The city is asleep, or pretending to be. I step out. The air is cold and wet, a physical weight against the skin.

The first thing is the silence. Not the absence of sound, but the presence of a specific kind of quiet that feels like held breath. The fog is here, of course. It is not the romantic mist of postcards. It is a thick, grey wool that erases the horizon. The Golden Gate Bridge, that red icon of American optimism, is just a vague smudge in the distance, like a bruise on the eye of the sky.

I walk north. My shoes slap against the pavement. The sound is too loud. It echoes off the brick facades of the Financial District, where the banks have closed their eyes for the night. The buildings are monolithic, their windows dark, reflecting nothing. They look like the walls of a tomb.

There is a line in a poem by W.H. Auden, "The more love, the more death; the more light, the more shadow." It feels appropriate here. The streetlights are sodium-vapor orange, casting long, distorted shadows that stretch out ahead of me like fingers. When I walk through them, they seem to grab at my ankles. I am moving through a world that is half-imagined. The fog makes the next ten feet the only reality that exists. The rest is potential.

I turn onto a hill. The grade is steep. My heart rate rises. It is a physical effort just to maintain momentum. The city is designed to exhaust you. It is a labyrinth that knows you are in it. I pass a row of Victorian houses, painted in pastel colors that have faded to a sickly gray. They look like teeth in a giant, sleeping mouth. A single window on the third floor of one of them is lit. A yellow square. I stop and look at it. There is no one there. The light is on, but the room is empty. It is a lure.

The feeling of the end of the world is not apocalyptic in the loud sense. There are no fires, no sirens. It is a quiet, bureaucratic ending. The lights are going out, one by one. The sun is not rising; it is bleeding. A thin line of pink appears at the top of the fog, a wound that will not heal. The air smells of salt and diesel.

I think about the concept of the "edge." In a flat city, the edge is the city limit, the place where the suburbs begin. Here, the edge is the water. The fog is the edge. The night is the edge. I am walking on the rim of a cliff that I cannot see.

A car passes. The headlights cut through the mist, blinding me for a second. When my vision clears, the car is gone. I am alone. The loneliness is not social; it is structural. The city is so large and so indifferent that my presence is a rounding error. I am a speck of dust on a lens.

I remember a line from a different poem, by Rainer Maria Rilke: "You must change your life." It is the most useless advice ever written, but it feels urgent now. To change the life, you have to leave the place. But I am here. I am walking. The fog is lifting slightly, revealing the true shape of the city. It is not a grid. It is a cluster. A tangle. A nervous system exposed.

The sun breaks the horizon. It does not rise; it bursts. The light hits the fog and turns it gold, then white, then hard and blue. The shadows retreat. The buildings solidify. The illusion breaks. The world is not ending. It is just waking up. The buses will start to run. The doors will open. The people will pour out, complaining about the cold, checking their phones, moving with the purposeful urgency of the living.

I turn around. The hill behind me is now a wall of light. I have to climb back down. The effort is the same. The gravity is the same. But the fear is gone, replaced by a dull, grinding fatigue. The city is just a city. It is expensive, it is hilly, and it is cold. I find a café. The coffee is burnt. The light is harsh. I sit down and watch the people arrive, and for a moment, I am one of them. The edge has receded. The world has continued.

prompt: Tell the origin story of how a musician selling his own CD online accidentally started a business. Write it as a blog post.
response:
The year is 1998. You are a bassist in a band that plays in basements where the carpet smells like wet dog. You have a CD-R burned on your laptop. It costs you four dollars to press. It takes you twenty minutes to burn. You want to sell it to the forty people who stood in the back of the basement last night.

You could go to a record store. But the store owner says he wants 30% off the top, and he only buys twenty copies. You say no.

You could go to a music distributor. They say, "We need 1,000 copies minimum, and here is a contract that says you owe us money if we don't sell them." You say no.

You have a website. It is a GeoCities page with a marquee that says "NEW EP COMING SOON." It has a contact form. You email the forty people. "Hey, the new record is out. I can mail you a copy for $15. Here is my address and my bank account number for a check. Or I can take your credit card over the phone."

You take the calls. You write the checks. You put the CDs in bubble mailers. You drive to the post office.

This is not a business. This is a job. You are a mail clerk. You are a customer service rep. You are a bookkeeper. You are a warehouse.

You sell out the forty copies. You make $600. You spend $100 on postage and bubble wrap. You keep $500. You buy a new set of strings.

Now, here is the mistake most people make when they look at this. They think the "business" starts when you get rich. They think the business starts when you have an office. They think the business starts when you hire a manager.

No. The business started the moment you separated the producer from the distributor.

For two centuries, the model was vertical integration. The studio owned the recording. The studio owned the pressing plant. The studio owned the distribution trucks. The studio owned the store shelves. You the artist were a wage laborer in this machine. You wrote the song. The machine took it. The machine made the money. You got a royalty check that arrived six months late and was 50 cents on the dollar.

In 1998, with a CD-R drive and a postal address, you broke the chain. You were the producer. You were the distributor. You were the store. You kept the margin.

But here is the hard part. Here is the part the success stories skip.

Selling 40 CDs is easy. Selling 4,000 is hell.

When you have 40 customers, you know their names. You know who is a fan and who is a tourist. You can handwrite a thank you note. It takes an hour. It feels like community.

When you have 4,000 customers, you cannot handwrite 4,000 notes. You cannot take 4,000 phone calls. You cannot drive to the post office 4,000 times. You cannot verify 4,000 credit cards without getting flagged for fraud.

At this point, you have two choices.

Choice A: You stop. You go back to the record label. You say, "Take 70%. Handle the mail. Handle the phone. Handle the fraud." You give up the margin to buy back your time. This is the "selling out" that people talk about. But it is actually just outsourcing.

Choice B: You build systems.

You buy a credit card processor. It takes 3% and 25 cents. You are still ahead of the label, because the label takes 70% and charges you for the marketing.

You buy a shipping service. You use a flat rate box. You stop driving to the post office. You put a sign in your window that says "UPS Pickup Here."

You hire a person. Not an executive. A person. A college kid who needs a job. You pay them $12 an hour. They answer the phone. They pack the boxes. They deal with the angry customer who says the CD arrived scratched.

Now you have a business. Not because you made more money. You probably made less money per CD than you did in the basement days. But you made it at scale. And you kept the rights.

The music industry in the 2000s spent a decade trying to kill this model. They sued Napster. They sued LimeWire. They sued individual teenagers. They tried to make the act of copying a file a crime.

They failed. Not because people were pirates. People are lazy. They wanted the music to be as easy to get as water.

The musicians who survived did not fight the pirates. They looked at the CD you sold in 1998. They realized that the value was not in the plastic disc. The value was in the relationship.

The CD was just the proof of purchase for the relationship.

So they stopped selling CDs. They started selling tickets. They started selling t-shirts. They started selling access. They used the website you built in 1998 to email the 4,000 people. "We are coming to your city. Here is a presale code."

The presale code was the new CD. It was a piece of data, not plastic. It had no cost to produce. It had infinite margin. And it was tied directly to the person who bought it.

This is the origin story. It is not a story about technology. It is not a story about file sharing. It is a story about a musician who decided to keep the margin, and then had to figure out how to do the job of a corporation alone, and then had to figure out how to outsource the parts of the job he didn't want to do, and then realized that the product was the relationship, not the artifact.

The accident was not that he started a business. The accident was that he realized the business was the only thing that made sense. The music was just the reason people paid attention.

You can still do this today. You don't need a website. You need a phone number. You need a way to take money. You need a way to deliver value.

The label still exists. The distributor still exists. The store still exists. They are all middlemen. They are all offering to take your margin in exchange for your time.

The question is not whether you can start a business. You can. It is just you, a phone, and a promise.

The question is whether you can handle the mail.

prompt: Write an essay about what it means for a category or definition to be wrong. Can you ever say a word like 'fish' or 'planet' is used incorrectly, or is it all convention? Use whatever examples you like, and carry the argument through to a place where it actually matters in real life.
response:
The word "wrong" usually implies a binary error, like a calculation that yields 2+2=5. But categories do not work like arithmetic. They are tools for navigation. When we ask if a definition is "wrong," we are not asking if it violates a metaphysical law. We are asking if the tool has broken, or if it is the wrong tool for the job at hand.

Consider the word "fish." In common parlance, a whale is not a fish. In biology, a whale is a mammal. This is not a convention we could vote to change tomorrow. It is a fact of evolutionary history. If you call a whale a fish, you are not using a different dialect; you are making a false claim about the animal’s physiology. You are ignoring the fact that it breathes air, nurses its young, and is warm-blooded. In this sense, definitions can be objectively wrong because they fail to track real, observable distinctions in the world.

However, the hard cases are not whales. They are things like "chair" or "planet."

Take "chair." If I sit on a beanbag, is it a chair? If I sit on a rock, is it a chair? The word "chair" does not have a precise set of necessary and sufficient conditions that every instance must meet and every non-instance must fail. It is a prototype. A wooden armchair is a "central" chair. A stool is a peripheral chair. A hammock is not a chair. The boundary is fuzzy.

Does this mean any usage is valid? No. If you point to a table and say, "That is a chair," you are not stretching the metaphor. You are failing to communicate. The category "chair" exists to solve a specific problem: identifying objects designed for sitting. When we stop using the word to solve that problem, the word becomes "wrong" not because it violates nature, but because it violates the shared purpose of the language.

This brings us to the definition of a "planet." For centuries, "planet" meant "wanderer"—any object that moves against the background of fixed stars. Under that definition, Earth is a planet, and the Moon is not. Then, with better telescopes, we discovered that Uranus, Neptune, and Pluto were also wanderers. They were planets.

In 2006, the International Astronomical Union (IAU) redefined "planet." They added a new criterion: a planet must "clear the neighborhood around its orbit." Pluto, which shares its orbital zone with thousands of other icy bodies in the Kuiper Belt, failed this test. It was demoted to a "dwarf planet."

Was this definition "wrong"?

If you ask a geologist, the answer is yes. Geologists care about composition and formation. Pluto is a solid, icy world with mountains, a subsurface ocean, and a complex atmosphere. It formed in the same way Earth did, by accreting from a protoplanetary disk. To a geologist, the IAU definition is arbitrary and useless. It draws a line based on orbital mechanics that has nothing to do with what a planet *is* in terms of physical structure. If the IAU had decided that to be a planet, an object must be at least 5,000 kilometers in diameter, we would have lost Mars and Jupiter from the category. The definition would have been wrong for anyone trying to study planetary science.

But the IAU was not trying to satisfy geologists. They were trying to satisfy educators and the public. The problem they were solving was classification for a solar system model. In a classroom, you need a clean, mutually exclusive category. If Pluto is a planet, then Ceres is a planet, and Haumea is a planet, and eventually, the word "planet" loses its power to distinguish the eight large, dominant worlds from the debris field. The IAU definition is "wrong" for geology, but "right" for solar system organization.

This is where the argument moves from philosophy to real life. Categories are not just descriptions; they are levers for action.

Consider the definition of "adult." In most legal systems, an adult is someone who is 18 years old. Is this definition "wrong"? Biologically, yes. The human brain does not finish developing until the mid-twenties. The prefrontal cortex, which handles impulse control and long-term planning, is still maturing at 18. If you define "adult" as someone capable of full rational self-governance, the legal definition is wrong. It misidentifies the state of the person.

Does it matter? Yes. Because the category "adult" triggers a specific set of rights and responsibilities: voting, signing contracts, drinking alcohol, and serving on juries. If the definition is wrong—if it includes people who are not cognitively ready for those responsibilities—then the system produces bad outcomes. We see this in the high rate of impulse-driven accidents among 18-to-21-year-old drivers. We see it in the vulnerability of young people to exploitative contracts. The error in the definition creates a gap between the law’s intent (to protect those who cannot protect themselves) and its execution.

This is not a minor semantic quibble. The definition of "adult" determines who is sent to juvenile court and who is sent to adult prison. In many US states, 17-year-olds are charged as adults for violent crimes. The biological reality is that a 17-year-old’s brain is structurally different from an adult’s in ways that affect culpability. If we define "adult" by a calendar date rather than by cognitive capacity, we are using a wrong tool. We are treating a continuum as a binary. The result is a justice system that punishes people for actions they were not fully neurologically equipped to avoid.

The same logic applies to medical definitions. For decades, "heart attack" was defined by a drop in blood pressure and specific changes on an EKG. This definition was "wrong" in a practical sense because it missed a large class of patients, particularly women and the elderly, who had heart attacks that did not present with those specific signs. The old definition created a gap in treatment. When the definition was updated to include biomarkers like troponin levels, the category tracked the physical reality of myocardial injury more accurately. The change in definition saved lives because it aligned the category with the pathology.

So, can a word be used incorrectly?

Yes, if the usage severs the connection between the word and the problem it is meant to solve.

If you call a whale a fish, you are wrong because you ignore the biological distinction that matters for marine ecology.
If you call a table a chair, you are wrong because you ignore the functional distinction that matters for furniture design.
If you call a 17-year-old an adult in a criminal trial, you are wrong because you ignore the neurological distinction that matters for fair sentencing.

The "wrongness" is not in the air. It is in the friction. When a definition is right, it fits the object or the situation with low resistance. It allows us to predict, plan, and act. When a definition is wrong, it creates drag. It forces us to make exceptions. It leads to misclassification, and misclassification leads to error.

We often think of language as a mirror, reflecting reality. It is not. Language is a net. We cast the net into the world and see what we catch. A "wrong" definition is a net with holes in the wrong places. It lets the important things slip through and catches the trivial things instead.

The IAU’s definition of a planet has holes. It lets the physical nature of Pluto slip through. But for the purpose of mapping the solar system, the net works. It catches the eight major bodies.

The legal definition of an adult has holes. It lets the biological reality of brain development slip through. For the purpose of administering justice, the net is failing. It catches people who are not yet ready for the weight of adult responsibility.

We can change the net. We can define "adult" by cognitive assessment rather than age. We can define "planet" by geology rather than orbit. The question is never "what is the true meaning?" The question is "what problem are we trying to solve, and does this category help us solve it?" If the answer is no, the definition is wrong. Not morally wrong, and not logically impossible, but practically wrong. And in real life, that is the only kind of wrong that costs anything.

prompt: Use a thought experiment about a town founded by people who hate late-night noise to think through when a community has the right to restrict what its members do, and then apply it to the housing and NIMBY debate. Write it as a long, exploratory blog post with a libertarian-ish flavor, ending with a practical proposal.
response:
# The Town of Quiet: A Thought Experiment on the Limits of Community

Imagine a town called Quieta. It is not a real place, but it is a useful one.

The founders of Quieta were a specific kind of person: shift workers, insomniacs, and people who simply valued sleep above all else. When they bought their land, they did so with a shared, explicit understanding. They paid a premium for land that was zoned exclusively for single-family residential use. They bought the silence. They bought the guarantee that no one would build a nightclub, a factory, or a duplex next to their house.

For the first fifty years, Quieta worked. The population grew slowly. Everyone agreed on the rules: no commercial activity after 10 PM, no multi-unit dwellings, no heavy industry. The value of the property held because the promise of quiet was kept.

Then, fifty years later, a young woman named Mara moves to Quieta. She is a teacher. She is not a shift worker. She does not have the same existential relationship with sleep that the founders did. She wants to rent out her spare room to a graduate student to help pay her mortgage. She also wants to open a small, late-night coffee shop in the garage of her home.

The neighbors of Quieta are outraged. They cite the founding compact. They argue that if Mara is allowed to run a coffee shop, next door will be a bakery, then a bar, then a hotel. The silence will be gone. The value of their homes will crash. They invoke the concept of "community standards." They argue that Mara is free to do whatever she wants, but only as long as she does not harm the community. They say her coffee shop is a harm.

This scenario is the core of the modern housing debate, stripped of the noise. It is the NIMBY (Not In My Backyard) argument in its purest form. And it is a libertarian’s nightmare, not because libertarians hate quiet, but because they recognize that the boundary between "my rights" and "our rights" is where tyranny begins.

To understand why, we have to look closely at the difference between a contract and a command.

### The Problem of the Moving Target

The founders of Quieta had a right to buy quiet. That was a transaction. They paid for a specific environment. If they wanted to keep that environment, they had to buy it from the people who moved in later. They could not buy it once and then demand that the market freeze in time.

Here is the hardest objection to the libertarian view, and we must take it seriously: **Externalities.**

If Mara builds a nightclub, the noise does not just affect her. It affects her neighbors. Sound waves do not respect property lines. If the nightclub generates a decibel level that physically disturbs the sleep of the person next door, the person next door has a legitimate claim. This is not a preference conflict; it is a physical invasion. In a pure libertarian framework, this is a tort. The neighbor can sue for damages. They can get an injunction to stop the noise. But they cannot ban the building.

The distinction is critical. If the building itself is the problem, then the neighbors are trying to ban a thing, not stop a wrong.

In Quieta, the neighbors do not just want to stop the noise. They want to stop the *existence* of the coffee shop. They want to prevent the change in land use. They are arguing that the "character" of the town is a shared asset that belongs to the current residents, and that Mara’s actions are a theft of that asset.

But who owns the "character" of the town?

If I buy a house in Quieta today, I do not own the history of the town. I do not own the silence of 1975. I own my plot of land. I own my right to speak, to assemble, and to use my property. The only thing I can claim is that my neighbors cannot make so much noise that it crosses my property line and disrupts my life. I cannot claim that they cannot *be* different from me.

### The Economics of Exclusion

Why do people in Quieta hate Mara? It is not really about the coffee. It is about price.

When a town restricts supply, it drives up price. By banning multi-unit dwellings and commercial use, Quieta has artificially limited the amount of housing available. This means that the people who can afford to live there are the people who can afford the premium for exclusivity. The founders paid for exclusivity. The current residents are benefiting from it. They are enjoying the appreciation of their property values, which is driven directly by the scarcity of housing.

Mara’s desire to build a duplex or open a shop is an attempt to break the price umbrella. If she is allowed to build a duplex, she can sell one unit and keep the other, or rent both out. This increases the supply of housing in Quieta. The price of housing in Quieta drops. The current residents’ property values drop.

The NIMBY argument is, in economic terms, a cartel. It is a group of homeowners who have colluded, through zoning laws, to limit supply and protect their investment. They frame this protection as a moral duty to preserve "community," but the mechanism is pure price control.

This is where the libertarian flavor becomes uncomfortable. Libertarians generally support free markets. They support the right to trade. They support the right to contract. But in Quieta, the "market" has been frozen. The right to trade in housing is being suppressed by the local government, at the behest of a specific class of buyers who bought in early.

Is there a libertarian justification for this freeze?

Some might argue for "consent theory." The idea is that when you move to Quieta, you consent to the existing rules. You are bound by the social contract of the town. If you don’t like the quiet, you should move to a loud town.

This argument has a fatal flaw: it assumes that the rules were set by the current majority, or that they are fixed. They are not. The rules were set by the founders. But the founders are gone. The current residents did not vote to create the zoning laws; they inherited them. More importantly, consent theory cannot justify the coercion of a newcomer. Mara did not sign a contract with the founders of Quieta. She signed a lease or a deed with the current owner. She is not a party to the founding compact.

If Mara is not a party to the contract, the town cannot enforce the contract against her. The town is acting as an enforcer of a private agreement to which it is not a party. This is not community; it is a club. And clubs have a problem: they cannot exclude people who live inside the club.

### The Slippery Slope of "Character"

The argument for Quieta’s zoning is usually phrased in terms of "character." But "character" is a code word for "who lives here."

When a neighborhood says, "We don't want that kind of development," they almost always mean, "We don't want that kind of person."

The coffee shop in the garage is a proxy for the presence of students, of workers, of people who are not retirees, of people who are not wealthy enough to afford a detached single-family home. The zoning law is a proxy for a caste system.

The libertarian critique here is not that we should tear down every fence and let every town become a strip mall. The libertarian critique is that the *state* should not be the tool used to enforce these preferences.

If the neighbors of Quieta truly value silence, they have a market solution: they can buy the land next to Mara. They can buy her garage. They can negotiate a private easement that restricts noise levels in exchange for a payment to Mara. If Mara refuses to sell, the neighbors can sue her for specific torts—nuisance, trespass of sound waves—but they cannot ban her from using her own land for lawful purposes.

The market allows for the trading of externalities. If you want quiet, you pay for it. If you want convenience, you pay for it. The state does not need to decide which value is superior. The state only needs to define the property rights clearly: the right to own land, the right to use it, and the right to be free from physical invasion.

### The Housing Crisis is a Zoning Crisis

We can apply this thought experiment to the real world, and the numbers are damning.

In the United States, the shortage of housing is not primarily caused by a lack of land. It is caused by the refusal of local governments to allow land to be used for housing.

Consider San Francisco. The city is surrounded by land. It has hills, valleys, and water. But the city has zoned most of its land for single-family homes or low-density uses. The result is that a one-bedroom apartment in San Francisco costs more than a mansion in much of the country.

This is not a natural market outcome. It is the outcome of the "Quieta" effect. The people who live in San Francisco, specifically the people who own single-family homes, have a financial incentive to block new housing. If they allow a six-unit building to be built on the lot next to their house, the supply of housing increases, the price of their house drops, and their wealth decreases.

They protect their wealth by invoking "neighborhood character." They use the zoning code, which is a state power, to protect their private asset.

This is a violation of the rights of the people who are locked out. The young teacher, the nurse, the artist, the worker—they are being told that their right to live where they work is subordinate to the right of the current homeowner to keep their property value high.

From a libertarian perspective, this is a transfer of wealth. It is a subsidy from the poor to the rich, facilitated by the state. The poor pay higher rent because the state prevents the supply from rising. The rich gain higher equity because the state prevents the competition. The state is the thief, and the NIMBYs are the beneficiaries.

### The Hardest Objection: Safety and Infrastructure

I must address the strongest counter-argument: **Infrastructure and Public Goods.**

NIMBYs often argue that allowing high-density housing will overwhelm the schools, the roads, and the sewer systems. They argue that the current residents are already paying for these systems, and that new residents will free-ride on them without contributing to the costs.

This is a valid concern, but it is a fiscal problem, not a rights problem.

If a new development is going to strain the local school system, the solution is not to ban the development. The solution is to make the developer pay for the strain. This is called impact fees. Many libertarian-leaning economists support impact fees because they internalize the externalities.

If the new duplex puts ten more kids in the local school, the developer should pay the school district the cost of educating those kids. If the new traffic clogs the roads, the developer should pay for road expansion.

But in Quieta, and in most US cities, the developer is not allowed to pay. They are simply banned. The town says, "We don't care if you have the money to pay for the school expansion. We don't want the kids."

This reveals the true nature of the restriction. It is not about infrastructure. It is about exclusion. If it were about infrastructure, the town would accept the fee. But they don't. They want the money *and* the exclusion. They want to charge a toll on existence.

A libertarian system would replace the ban with a price. The right to live in Quieta should be purchasable. The price should reflect the true cost of the externalities: the noise, the traffic, the school seats. If Mara can pay the price, she should be allowed to live there. If she cannot, she cannot. But the barrier should be money, not prejudice.

### A Practical Proposal

So, what does a libertarian approach to zoning look like? It does not look like anarchy. It does not look like a warehouse next to a bedroom. It looks like a radical simplification of the law.

**1. Abolish Use Zoning, Keep Density Zoning.**
Zoning that dictates *what* you can do (residential, commercial, industrial) is a ban on trade. It is a cartel. It must go. You should be allowed to open a bakery, a daycare, a brewery, or a duplex on any lot.

However, we can keep regulations on *physical impact*. We can regulate height. We can regulate setbacks. We can regulate noise levels. We can regulate fire safety.

Why keep density? Because density is a physical externality. A 20-story tower blocks the sun and creates wind tunnels. It puts strain on the power grid. It changes the microclimate. These are measurable physical harms that affect neighbors. They can be regulated without banning the building.

A 20-story tower might be illegal in a residential zone because it blocks the light. A bakery might be illegal in a residential zone if it produces 80 decibels of noise at 3 AM. But a duplex? A duplex is not a physical harm. It is a choice. It is a trade.

**2. Private Easements and HOAs.**
If the neighbors of Quieta really want a town of single-family homes, they can create one. They can form a Homeowners Association (HOA) with binding covenants. They can restrict the sale of homes to people who agree to the covenants. They can maintain the green lawns. They can ban the coffee shop.

But they cannot force Mara to join the HOA if she does not own a home in it. And if Mara owns a home in it, she must have had the chance to opt out when she bought the house. If the covenant was attached to the deed, she knew the rules. If she didn’t know, she has a claim for fraud, not a right to break the rule.

The key is **opt-in**. Community standards must be chosen, not imposed.

**3. Impact Fees as the Only Barrier.**
If a new development causes a measurable cost to the public infrastructure, the developer pays. If a new school is needed, the developer pays. If a new road is needed, the developer pays. This is not a tax; it is a price. It ensures that the cost of living is borne by the person who chooses to live there, not by the people who are already there.

### The End of Quieta

The town of Quieta is a fantasy of the past. It is a place where the market was paused. It is a place where the preferences of the first 50 years were allowed to govern the next 50.

The reality is that communities change. People move. Needs shift. The "character" of a place is not a static object that can be preserved in amber. It is a living thing that is constantly being negotiated through trade.

When we say that a community has the right to restrict what its members do, we are saying that the past has a claim on the future. We are saying that the people who left are still in charge.

The libertarian answer is simple: You can buy quiet. You can buy exclusivity. You can build a wall. But you cannot buy the freedom of others. You cannot force the new neighbor to be the old neighbor. You cannot use the state to freeze the market and protect your equity.

Mara gets her coffee shop. The neighbors get their lawsuit for the noise, if the noise crosses the line. And the town gets what it deserves: a price tag on its own preferences.

If you can’t pay for the silence, you don’t own it. You’re just lucky you were born there.

prompt: Software teams keep arguing about who should write the spec and who should own product design. Write an essay about where that job should sit in an organization, who to hire for it, and who not to, drawing on any big-company experience you have.
response:
The argument usually starts with a title. A junior engineer complains that Product Management is a "feature request queue." A senior PM counters that Engineering is "solutioning first," hiding behind technical constraints to avoid doing the hard work of defining value. Both sides are often right about the other, and both are wrong about where the boundary actually lies.

The confusion stems from treating "spec" as a single artifact that gets passed over the wall. It is not. There are two distinct jobs that get conflated under that word, and they require different minds. The first is defining the problem: what pain exists, who has it, and what the outcome of solving it looks like. The second is defining the solution: how the system behaves, what the edge cases are, and how the data flows.

The problem definition must sit with Product. The solution definition must sit with Engineering. The moment you hand the problem definition to Engineering, you have hired a consultant to do a client’s job for them. The moment you hand the solution definition to Product, you have hired a project manager to do an architect’s job for them.

This is not a theoretical split. It is visible in the failure modes of big companies.

When Product owns the solution, the spec becomes a wireframe with behavioral rules. It says, "When the user clicks this button, the page reloads." It specifies the exact error message string. It dictates the database schema because the PM read a blog post about data models. The result is a brittle product. The engineering team, stripped of ownership, builds it exactly as specified. Then they leave. The next engineer arrives, sees the rigid structure, and finds it impossible to extend. The product stagnates because the interface between the business logic and the implementation is too thin. The PM has created a document that is 80% correct but 100% prescriptive.

When Engineering owns the problem, the spec becomes a technical roadmap. It says, "We will build a microservices architecture for the billing module." It optimizes for latency because the lead engineer cares about latency. It ignores that the sales team actually wants to export invoices to Excel, a feature that is trivial to build but critical to revenue. The result is a system that is technically impressive and commercially irrelevant. The engineering team is proud of the code. The customer is confused by the interface. The company burns six months of runway building the wrong thing.

So who writes the spec?

The spec should be written by the person who will be held accountable for the outcome, but it must be co-authored by the person who will be held accountable for the implementation. This sounds like a compromise. It is not. It is a division of labor based on information asymmetry.

The Product Manager holds the information about the customer. They know why the user is angry. They know which feature drives retention. They do not know if that feature can be built in four weeks or four months. They do not know if the current database can handle the load. If they try to guess, they make bad trade-offs.

The Engineering Lead holds the information about the system. They know the technical debt. They know the security risks. They do not know if the feature matters. If they guess, they build the wrong thing.

The artifact that results from this collaboration is not a document. It is a contract. The Product Manager writes the "Why" and the "What." They define the success metrics. They define the non-goals. They say, "We need to reduce checkout abandonment by 10%." They say, "We are not building a mobile app this quarter." They do not say how the checkout works.

The Engineering Lead writes the "How." They define the technical approach. They identify the risks. They say, "To get that 10% reduction, we need to refactor the payment gateway. It will take six weeks, not four. There is a risk that the legacy code will break existing enterprise clients. We propose a phased rollout."

The meeting where these two meet is the spec. The document that comes out of it is a summary for the rest of the team. It is not the source of truth. The source of truth is the shared understanding between the PM and the Eng Lead. If the document says "use a modal" and the Eng Lead knows a modal will cause accessibility issues, the Eng Lead changes it. If the document says "show all products" and the PM knows the customer only wants the top three, the PM changes it.

This requires a specific kind of hiring.

You do not want a Product Manager who thinks they are a designer. You want a Product Manager who is comfortable with ambiguity. The best PMs I have seen in large organizations are not the ones with the most polished slides. They are the ones who can walk into a room with a backend engineer and a frontend engineer, and ask questions that reveal the hidden constraints. They are curious about the data. They are suspicious of the status quo. They can say, "I don't know if this is the right feature, but here is what the data suggests, and here is what the user said. Help me figure out if this is worth building."

You do not want an Engineering Lead who thinks they are a project manager. You want an Engineering Lead who is comfortable with uncertainty.
