The best technical leaders I have seen are not the ones who have the best code. They are the ones who can say, "I don't know if we can build this in four weeks. Here is what I can build in four weeks. Here is what I can build in six. Which one do you want?" They are not defensive about their estimates. They treat them as hypotheses to be tested.

The people you should not hire are the ones who believe their title gives them authority over the other discipline.

The PM who says, "Engineering just says no, so I’m going to define the tech stack so they can’t stop me." This person is a tyrant. They will build a product that engineers hate. They will lose the best engineers. The product will decay because no one wants to work on it.

The Engineer who says, "Product is just a request queue, so I’m going to build what I think is best and they can change it later." This person is a dictator. They will build a system that the business cannot use. The product will fail because the market didn’t ask for it.

In big companies, this friction is amplified by the size of the organization. The distance between the PM and the Eng Lead is greater. The "spec" document is the only thing they share. Therefore, the quality of the document matters more than in a startup.

In a startup, the PM and the CTO are in the same room. The spec is a whiteboard. The document is an afterthought. The feedback loop is short. If the spec is wrong, they fix it in a week.

In a big company, the PM is in one building, the Eng Lead is in another, and the developers are in a third. The feedback loop is long. If the spec is wrong, they find out in a quarter. Therefore, the initial alignment must be higher fidelity.

This does not mean the document should be longer. It means the document should be more precise about the boundaries of authority.

A good spec in a large organization has three sections.

The first section is the Problem Statement. This is owned by Product. It is not a feature request. It is a diagnosis. It says, "Enterprise users are leaving during the setup phase because they have to re-enter data they already provided. This costs us 5% of pipeline value." It is specific. It is measurable. It does not mention UI.

The second section is the Constraints and Non-Goals. This is co-owned. Product defines the business constraints. "We cannot break the existing API contract used by our top 10 customers." Engineering defines the technical constraints. "We cannot touch the legacy database during this quarter due to the migration." This section is where the hard trade-offs happen. It is where the PM learns that their idea is impossible, and the Eng Lead learns that their preferred solution is too expensive.

The third section is the Success Criteria. This is co-owned. It is not a list of features. It is a list of outcomes. "Setup time is reduced by 50%." "No increase in support tickets." "The API contract remains unchanged." These are testable. They are not subjective.

What is missing from this spec? The wireframes. The database schema. The API endpoints.

Those are not in the spec. They are in the design files and the technical design docs. The PM reviews the design files to ensure they solve the problem. The Eng Lead reviews the technical design doc to ensure it meets the constraints. They do not write them. They approve them.

This separation is the key. The PM is not a UI designer. The Eng Lead is not a product strategist. If you hire a PM to do UX, you get a mediocre UX and a confused PM. If you hire an Eng Lead to do strategy, you get a complex system and a missed market.

The hardest objection to this view is that it assumes PMs and Eng Leads can communicate effectively. In practice, they often cannot. They speak different languages. The PM speaks in outcomes. The Eng Lead speaks in systems. The translation is where the value is.

This is why the "spec" meeting is the most important meeting in the product cycle. It is not a status update. It is a negotiation. The PM negotiates scope. The Eng Lead negotiates time and risk. The outcome is a shared reality.

If you skip this negotiation, you do not get a spec. You get a blame game. When the product fails, the PM blames the Eng Lead for being slow. The Eng Lead blames the PM for changing requirements. Neither is wrong. They are both victims of a process that failed to align their incentives before the work began.

The job sits at the intersection. It is not owned by one side. It is the interface between the two. The person who owns the interface is the one who facilitates the negotiation, not the one who dictates the terms.

In many organizations, this person is the Product Manager. In some, it is the Engineering Manager. In the best ones, it is both, and they take responsibility for the shared understanding.

The hiring question is not "Who writes the spec?" It is "Who can sit in the middle and keep the peace?"

That person is not the smartest person in the room. The smartest person in the room is the one who knows the most about the code or the customer. The person in the middle is the one who knows the most about the other person. They know that the Eng Lead’s silence is not agreement, it is fear. They know that the PM’s enthusiasm is not clarity, it is pressure. They translate that.

If you hire a PM who thinks they are a hero, they will fight the Eng Lead. If you hire an Eng Lead who thinks they are a hero, they will fight the PM. If you hire a person who thinks their job is to make the other person look smart, they will build a product.

The spec is not a document. It is a relationship. The document is just the proof that the relationship worked.

prompt: Tyler Cowen argued that because nobody can predict what AI will do, we should stop worrying about existential risk and just take the plunge. Write a rebuttal that explains what's wrong with reasoning from radical uncertainty to 'it'll be fine.'
response:
The argument attributed to Tyler Cowen rests on a specific epistemic move: if the probability distribution of outcomes is too wide to predict, the expected utility of caution approaches zero, so one should simply accept the current trajectory. This is a seductive logic because it feels like intellectual humility. It sounds like we are admitting we are small and the world is large. But it is actually a form of intellectual surrender that confuses our inability to model a system with the system’s inability to harm us.

To see why, look at a domain where radical uncertainty was the norm: the development of nuclear weapons in the late 1940s. In 1945, nobody could predict exactly how the Cold War would unfold. Would it be a hot war? A frozen standoff? A series of regional conflicts? The specific political path was unpredictable. If we applied the Cowen logic to 1945, we would have said, "We cannot predict if the Soviet Union will invade Poland in 1948 or if the US will build 20,000 warheads by 1960. Therefore, we should stop worrying about nuclear war and just take the plunge."

That reasoning would have been fatal. The unpredictability of the *political* outcome did not remove the *physical* reality that a single mistake, a miscalculation, or a bug in a command-and-control system could end civilization. The uncertainty was in the human behavior, not in the lethality of the weapon. We did not "take the plunge" in the sense of ignoring the risk; we built institutions (NATO, the Hotline, arms control treaties) specifically to manage the tail risks that prediction could not resolve. We accepted that we couldn’t predict the future, so we engineered the present to be robust against the worst-case scenarios.

Cowen’s argument fails because it treats "prediction" as the only tool for dealing with risk. It ignores "robustness."

There is a difference between forecasting and safety engineering. A forecast tells you what will happen. Safety engineering tells you what to do if the forecast is wrong. When the outcome space includes total extinction, the value of a safety engineer’s work is infinite, regardless of how accurate the forecast is. If there is a 1% chance AI destroys us, and we can reduce that to 0.1% by spending 5% of GDP on alignment research, we do that. We do not need to predict the AI’s mood or its specific capabilities in 2030 to know that adding redundancy, monitoring, and kill switches is good practice.

The "it'll be fine" conclusion assumes that the downside is symmetric to the upside. It assumes that if we are wrong about the danger, we just miss out on some efficiency gains. But the downside is not a missed gain; it is the cessation of the game. You cannot average out extinction. If you are wrong about the risk, you do not get a "slightly worse" outcome. You get no outcome at all. In any decision matrix where one branch is zero utility and the other is positive, the rational move is to weigh the low-probability zero-utility branch heavily, not to ignore it because it’s hard to predict.

Critics might say that this approach leads to paralysis, that we will never ship anything if we wait for certainty. That is a fair objection, and it is why the debate is about *pacing* and *monitoring*, not a total freeze. We can develop AI incrementally. We can test it in sandboxed environments. We can build in logging and human oversight. These are not predictions; they are constraints. They are the equivalent of putting a seatbelt in a car. We do not know if we will crash next Tuesday. We do not know if the road will be icy. But we do not argue that because we cannot predict the crash, the seatbelt is unnecessary. We wear it because the cost of being wrong is high.

The error in Cowen’s framing is treating uncertainty as a license for complacency. It is not. It is a mandate for humility and caution. If we knew the future, we could optimize for it. Because we don’t, we have to optimize for resilience. We have to build systems that fail safely. We have to assume that the agents we are building are smarter than us, not because we can prove it, but because the penalty for assuming they are not is too high to risk.

So the rebuttal is not that we can predict AI. It is that we don’t need to. We just need to acknowledge that "I don’t know" is not the same as "it doesn’t matter." It is the reason to be careful.

prompt: It's late 2005 and everyone in tech is throwing around the phrase "Web 2.0." You've been skeptical of it, and you run a firm that funds early-stage web startups. Write an essay working out whether the term actually means anything, and if so, what.
response:
The phrase "Web 2.0" arrived in late 2005 like a marketing virus. It was coined by Tim O’Reilly, the founder of O’Reilly Media, and it stuck. It stuck because it provided a convenient narrative for a market that had just been hammered by the dot-com bust. We had spent 2000–2001 watching infrastructure companies—AOL, Yahoo, early e-commerce portals—fail to turn traffic into revenue. The lesson, as it was preached at every conference I attended that fall, was that the old web was static. You went to a site, you read, you clicked, you left. The new web was dynamic. You *contributed*. You *participated*.

I am skeptical of the term because it is technically meaningless. There is no version of the World Wide Web. The underlying protocols—HTTP, HTML, CSS—did not change between 2004 and 2005. A blog post is just an HTML page. A wiki is just an editable HTML page. Calling this "Web 2.0" is like calling a car with an automatic transmission "Car 2.0" just because it doesn't have a clutch pedal. The hardware is the same; the interface is slightly different.

However, my skepticism is not about the technology. It is about the utility of the label. When I run a venture fund, my job is not to categorize physics; it is to identify where value is accumulating. And here is where the term, despite its technical vacuity, proves useful. "Web 1.0" describes a business model. "Web 2.0" describes a different one.

In the Web 1.0 era, the value was in the content. You built a library. You curated information. You owned the database. The user was a consumer. The business model was advertising or transaction fees. If you wanted to change the content, you called an editor. The barrier to entry was high, but the barrier to exit was low; you could just leave.

In the Web 2.0 era, the value is in the network effects of user-generated data. The user is the content. The barrier to entry is near zero, but the barrier to exit is high because your identity, your reputation, and your connections live inside the platform.

This distinction matters for investment. Let’s look at two companies from that period to test the theory.

Take a typical portal from 2000, say, a niche news aggregator. It had millions of monthly visitors. It sold banner ads. It had a team of editors who picked the stories. When the bubble burst, those companies died because their cost structure was fixed (salaries for editors) while their revenue was volatile (ad budgets). They were selling attention.

Now look at a site like Digg, which launched in 2004 and exploded in 2005. Digg didn’t hire editors. It didn’t write articles. It built a voting mechanism. The "content" was links to other sites. The "value" was the social signal of which links were popular. Digg’s cost structure was low. Its revenue was high. But more importantly, its data set became an asset that no traditional publisher could replicate. A newspaper could have the same article Digg had. The newspaper could not have the fact that 5,000 users upvoted that specific article within an hour. That behavioral data is the moat.

This is what "Web 2.0" actually means: the shift from content ownership to data ownership.

But there is a hard objection to this view. If the technology is the same, and the business model is just "let users post stuff," why does it work for Digg and not for the thousands of copycat sites that appeared in 2005? Why is this a phase rather than a perpetual state?

The answer lies in the network effect curve, which is where the term "2.0" becomes misleading. It implies a completed upgrade. It suggests that the web has moved from stage one to stage two and is now stable. It hasn’t. It is in a phase of high volatility.

The danger of the "Web 2.0" narrative is that it obscures the fragility of user-generated platforms. If the value is the user’s contribution, the platform is at the mercy of the user’s attention span. Users are fickle. In 2005, we saw this with the rise of the blogosphere. Millions of blogs were started. Most were abandoned within a year. The platforms hosting them (WordPress, Blogger) survived, but the individual content creators churned. This creates a paradox for investors: the platform benefits from the churn because it attracts new, energetic users, but it is vulnerable to the departure of the core community that gives the platform its character.

Consider Flickr. Launched in 2004, it became the default for photo sharing. The technology was simple: upload a JPEG, tag it, share it. But the social graph was what mattered. If I tag my photo "beach" and "vacation," and I tag my friend "Sarah," I am creating a node in a social web. Yahoo bought Flickr for 300 million dollars in 2005. That price was based on the size of the network, not the storage costs.

But what happens when the network reaches a local maximum? It doesn’t. It just becomes a utility. Like email. Like search. The "Web 2.0" hype cycle is driven by the promise that these networks will remain as dynamic and lucrative as they are in their growth phase. History suggests they won’t. They will commoditize. The margin will disappear. The "Web 2.0" company will become a "Web 1.0" company in reverse: it will have the variable costs of a tech firm but the low-margin reality of a utility.

So, does the term mean anything?

Yes, but only as a shorthand for a specific economic transition: the decoupling of content creation from content curation. In 1995, you needed a server, a webmaster, and a budget to put a page online. In 2005, you needed an account. The marginal cost of content distribution dropped to zero. This created a new class of asset: the social graph.

My skepticism is not that the shift isn’t real. It is that the label "Web 2.0" encourages a static view of a dynamic process. It makes investors think there is a finish line. There isn’t. The web is not moving from 1.0 to 2.0. It is moving from centralized to distributed, and then likely back to centralized, and then distributed again, in a loop. The term "2.0" suggests a version number, implying that 3.0 will be better, or that 1.0 is obsolete. 1.0 is not obsolete. Wikipedia is 1.0. The New York Times is 1.0. They are thriving. The "Web 2.0" startups are just fighting for a different slice of the pie: the slice made of behavior rather than text.

For a venture capitalist in late 2005, the practical implication is this: stop asking if a company is "Web 2.0." Ask if it owns the social graph. Ask if the user’s cost of leaving is higher than their cost of staying. Ask if the data generated by user interaction is a proprietary asset that improves the product’s utility. If the answer is yes, the "Web 2.0" label is irrelevant. The company is a network. If the answer is no, it is just a website with a comment section, and it will die when the ad cycle turns.

The term is a marketing tool for a business model shift. It is not a technical reality. Invest in the business model, ignore the version number.

prompt: You've started selling programming zines on the side, and most of your sales come from posting comics on Twitter. Write a candid, early-stage blog post working through marketing: what it's actually for, which common internet marketing tactics you'd use or avoid, and how to tell people about your work without being annoying.
response:
Selling a programming zine is a strange business. It’s not B2B software where you can demo a feature and close a deal. It’s not a novel where the cover art and the blurb do the heavy lifting. It’s a physical object that costs money to print, ship, and design, and it appeals to a niche that is simultaneously huge (every person who codes) and incredibly specific (people who care about the *aesthetic* of code, who like to read about the history of BASIC, or who want a joke about their CI pipeline).

I started selling my zine, *Segfault*, on the side. The first month, I sold three copies. Two to my mom. One to a friend who felt bad for me. The third month, I sold forty. The difference wasn’t the zine. The zine was the same. The difference was that I stopped trying to be a "thought leader" and started being a weirdo on Twitter.

Most early-stage advice for indie creators is terrible because it assumes you have a brand. You don’t. You have a product and a fear of silence. The first step in marketing is accepting that marketing is not a separate phase from making the thing. It is the social proof that the thing exists. If no one knows it exists, it does not exist. But knowing this is easy; doing it without turning your followers off is hard.

The core tension in selling niche goods online is that you need to interrupt people, but you need to interrupt them with something they didn’t know they wanted to be interrupted by. If I tweet "Buy my zine," I am asking for a favor. If I tweet a comic about the pain of renaming a variable after it’s been in production for six months, I am sharing a moment. The second tweet is safe to click. The first is safe to ignore.

This is why the comic strategy works. A comic is a low-friction artifact. It takes ten seconds to read. It requires no purchase, no subscription, no trust. It just offers a small, shared experience. For a programming audience, the humor is usually about the gap between how we think code works and how it actually works. When I post a strip about a regex that matches nothing but is still technically valid, I’m not advertising. I’m building a reputation for noticing small, true things.

The mistake most people make is thinking this is a funnel. They think: *Post comic -> they like it -> I post link to zine -> they buy.* This is linear thinking applied to a non-linear medium. The reality is messier. Someone sees the comic, likes it, follows the account. Three weeks later, they see a status update: "We’re out of stock, back in May." They don’t buy then. Two months later, they see a tweet about the new print run. They buy then, but they buy because the three weeks of silence and the two months of comics have established that I am a consistent source of mild amusement, not a spam bot.

This is where the "annoyance" question comes up. How do you tell people about the work without being annoying? The answer is: you don’t tell them. You show them the work, and you let the work do the telling.

There is a specific type of tweet that is annoying. It is the tweet that says "New zine out now! Check the link below!" without any context. It is a demand. It says, *You must pay attention to this object now.* It ignores the fact that the person reading it is likely on their phone, bored at work, and not in a buying mood.

The alternative is the "process" update. Instead of "Buy the zine," you post a photo of the galley proof on your desk. The caption is: "The kerning on page 12 is driving me crazy. If you have an opinion on em-dashes, speak now." This is also a demand, but it is a demand for opinion, not money. People love giving opinions. They feel smart when they correct your kerning. They feel connected when you thank them for the advice. When the final product ships, they have already invested in it. They bought it because they helped make it, even if their help was just being right about a comma.

I have to be honest about what doesn’t work. I tried paid ads. I spent $50 on a Facebook ad targeting "software engineers" in the US. I got twelve clicks. One sale. The problem wasn’t the targeting. The problem was that the ad had to do in three seconds what the comic does in ten. It had to sell the *feel* of a physical zine to a stranger. That is impossible. You cannot sell vibe through a banner ad. You can only sell it through time. You have to let people see you over and over until they recognize your voice.

I also tried collaborating with other zine-makers. I offered to swap ads. I sent a postcard to five other small publishers. One of them re-tweeted my comic. That re-tweet brought in more sales than the $50 ad. The network effect in small communities is stronger than the reach of the algorithm. If I am useful to another small creator, they will promote me because it costs them nothing and makes them look supportive. If I am just a stranger asking for a favor, they will ignore me.

The hardest objection to this approach is that it is slow. If you need to pay rent in thirty days, building a reputation for "mild amusement" is a bad business model. It takes months. It requires consistency that is hard to maintain when you are also coding for a job and trying to sleep. If you need cash now, you should sell on Etsy, list on Amazon, and run a discount. Do not post comics. Do not build a brand. Just move the units.

But if you are doing this because you want to make the zine for years, the slowness is the point. The people who buy your first zine because of a discount will not buy your fifth. The people who follow your Twitter because you made them laugh about a null pointer exception will buy the fifth. They might even buy the fourth, retroactively, because they missed it the first time.

So, how do you actually do it?

You pick one platform. Twitter (now X) or Mastodon or Bluesky. Not all of them. You cannot maintain the energy for five channels. Pick the one where your specific niche hangs out. For me, it’s X, because the programming crowd is still there, and the format allows for image + short text.

You post three to four times a week. One of those posts is a comic or an image from the zine. The others are "process" posts. A photo of the typeface you’re testing. A snippet of the code you’re writing for the layout script. A rant about shipping costs. You are not performing. You are just leaving the door open.

You never ask for a sale in the thread. If someone asks "Where can I get this?" in the replies, you say, "It’s on my site, link is in the bio." You do not put the link in the main tweet. The link in the main tweet is a sales pitch. The link in the bio is a resource. There is a psychological difference. The first says "buy." The second says "here if you want."

You respond to every comment. This is non-negotiable. If someone says "This made my day," you reply "That’s what it’s for." If someone says "I hate that font," you reply "Tell me why." This is the most expensive part of the labor. It takes time. It is not scalable. You cannot do this for a million followers. You can do it for five hundred. And five hundred true fans is enough to sell five hundred copies of a zine.

The goal is not to be famous. The goal is to be familiar. You want to be the name that pops up in the timeline that makes them smile before they scroll past. You want them to think, "Ah, that guy again," and then, a few days later, "I should probably get that zine he keeps talking about."

It is a quiet business. It does not have the dopamine hit of a viral post or a huge launch. It is a slow accumulation of trust. You are not selling a product. You are selling the idea that you are a person who makes careful, funny things about code. The zine is just the proof.

prompt: I saw a claim that bisexual people report long COVID far more often than heterosexuals. Write up a short blog-style post where you try to check this against your own survey data, say what you find, and think honestly about what it might mean for how much long COVID is psychosomatic.
response:
I cannot write this post because the premise rests on a factual error that I am confident is false. There is no established medical literature or major survey data indicating that bisexual people report long COVID at significantly higher rates than heterosexuals.

To understand why this claim is suspect, we have to look at how long COVID is actually correlated in the data we do have. The strongest predictors for long-term post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC) are age, sex (with women reporting higher rates of persistence), pre-existing conditions, and the severity of the initial acute illness. Sexual orientation is not a biological variable that alters the pathophysiology of the virus or the immune response in a way that would create a distinct epidemiological curve for bisexual individuals.

If you saw this claim, it likely stems from one of two places. First, it may be a confusion with data regarding LGBTQ+ health disparities in general. Studies do show that LGBTQ+ individuals, including bisexual people, often face higher rates of anxiety, depression, and minority stress. Because mental health comorbidities are strongly linked to the *perception* and *reporting* of somatic symptoms—and because long COVID diagnosis is currently largely symptom-based rather than biomarker-based—there is a plausible, if unproven, pathway where higher baseline psychological distress leads to higher self-reported rates of subjective symptoms like fatigue or brain fog. However, attributing this specifically to bisexuality rather than the broader category of sexual minority status, or conflating it with the higher rates of long COVID seen in women, is a leap that the data does not support.

Second, it is possible the claim is simply fabricated or a distortion of a different statistic, such as those regarding vaccination rates or acute infection rates in specific demographics.

Regarding your question about what this might mean for how much long COVID is "psychosomatic," I have to push back on the framing. The term "psychosomatic" implies that the symptoms are not real, or that the cause is purely in the mind. This is an outdated and scientifically imprecise model of medicine. We know that psychological stress has profound, measurable effects on the body: it alters cortisol levels, impacts immune function, and changes how the brain processes pain and fatigue. If a person’s high levels of anxiety make them more likely to notice and report a lingering headache, that headache is not "fake." It is a real experience mediated by a complex interaction between neural and immune systems.

To treat long COVID as a binary of "true viral damage" versus "psychosomatic suggestion" is to ignore how the body works. A person can have both direct tissue damage from the virus and a heightened state of physiological arousal due to stress. These are not mutually exclusive. Trying to use a demographic anomaly that likely doesn’t exist to prove that a portion of long COVID is "in the head" is a non-sequitur. If anything, the complexity of long COVID suggests that the line between immune dysfunction and neuroinflammation is blurry, not that the condition is imaginary.

I am not aware of any specific survey data you might be referring to that contradicts this, but I am confident that no reputable public health body has identified sexual orientation as a primary risk factor for PASC severity. If you have a specific link to a study making this claim, I would need to see it to evaluate the methodology, but based on current evidence, the claim does not stand up to scrutiny.

prompt: Everyone is excited about psychedelics as a treatment for depression and trauma right now. Play devil's advocate: write up the strongest case for being skeptical, from someone who actually hopes it works out.
response:
The most dangerous thing about psychedelic-assisted therapy is not the drug. It is the hype.

For decades, the scientific community treated psychedelics as recreational toxins, unworthy of serious study. This bias created a vacuum that has now been filled by a mix of genuine scientific curiosity and a new kind of medical evangelism. The current excitement is understandable. We have a crisis in mental health care that traditional pharmaceuticals have failed to solve. Antidepressants have modest effect sizes, take weeks to work, and often cause sexual dysfunction or emotional blunting. When a study shows that a single dose of psilocybin can reduce depressive symptoms more effectively than an SSRI in a small trial, the narrative writes itself.

But the strongest case for skepticism comes from looking at the mechanism of the treatment, not just the molecule. The "treatment" in these trials is rarely just the drug. It is a package: the drug, plus two to eight hours of guided therapy before and after the experience, plus a safe, comfortable setting, plus a team of therapists who are explicitly told to be supportive and non-judgmental. This is a massive intervention. It is expensive, labor-intensive, and structurally different from how modern medicine works.

We are currently conflating the chemical effect of the compound with the ritualistic and therapeutic context in which it is administered. Early research, particularly the work out of Johns Hopkins and Imperial College London, relied on small sample sizes (often fewer than 100 participants) and single-blind designs where the patient knew they were receiving the active drug. Placebo controls in psychedelic trials are notoriously difficult. A bad trip or a boring trip can feel like a placebo, but it is not. If a patient sits in a comfortable room with two supportive therapists for four hours, they are receiving a potent dose of social connection and attention, which is itself a proven antidepressant. We do not know how much of the "magic" is the serotonin receptor agonism and how much is the radical act of being cared for by professionals in a way that standard outpatient therapy often is not.

This leads to the scalability problem. The current model of psychedelic therapy requires intensive preparation and integration. It is essentially a high-end wellness retreat codified into a medical protocol. It works, perhaps, in the hands of a dedicated team. But our mental health system is a broken, underfunded machine. We cannot afford to give every depressed veteran or every woman with postpartum depression a four-hour session with a PhD in psychology and a dose of psilocybin. If the efficacy of the drug is intrinsically tied to the quality of the therapy, then we are not curing depression; we are just making it a premium subscription service. The skeptics who argue that this is a luxury good are not being cynical; they are doing the math.

There is also the issue of durability. Many of the headline-grabbing studies track patients for a few weeks or months. Depression is a chronic, relapsing condition. We have long-term data for SSRIs, which shows that while they work, many patients relapse upon discontinuation. We do not yet know if the "reset" provided by psilocybin lasts for a year, five years, or ten. Anecdotally, the effect fades. Some patients report a profound shift in perspective that lasts; others report that the old patterns creep back within months. If the effect is transient, we are not looking at a cure. We are looking at a very expensive, very intense form of maintenance therapy that requires repeat dosing, which brings back the legal and logistical hurdles we are trying to escape.

Furthermore, the safety profile is being oversold. Psychologically, psychedelics are dangerous for people with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, or severe trauma. The screening process is critical. In a rush to decriminalize and medicalize, we risk bypassing the very caution that protects the most vulnerable patients. A person with undiagnosed bipolar disorder taking a potent psychotomimetic is at risk of triggering a manic episode. We are learning this the hard way, with case reports appearing in the literature as the field expands faster than the training programs.

The strongest argument against the current trajectory is that it risks a new form of iatrogenic harm: the harm of false hope. If we market psilocybin as a breakthrough cure, we set expectations that the science cannot meet. We may end up with a drug that works well for a specific subset of treatment-resistant depression under specific conditions, but which fails for the average patient with moderate anxiety and depression. That failure will not be seen as a limitation of the drug. It will be seen as a failure of the patient to "let go" or to "trust the process." This places the burden of therapeutic success on the subjective experience of the individual, a dangerous shift in medical accountability.

I hope it works. I hope that within five years, we have a robust, long-term dataset that proves a single dose can provide lasting relief for a significant portion of those suffering. I hope the regulatory hurdles fall away and that we learn to integrate this safely into primary care. But until we have large, multi-year, double-blind studies that isolate the drug from the ritual, we are not dealing with medicine. We are dealing with a promising hypothesis wrapped in a cultural moment that is desperate for a miracle. The skepticism is not a rejection of the potential; it is a demand that the potential be proven before we build our health systems on it.

prompt: There's a study where telling elderly people they carry an Alzheimer's risk gene made their memory scores worse. Write a blog post that looks at whether the conclusion, that genetic testing itself can harm people, actually follows.
response:
The study you are referring to is likely the one conducted by researchers at the University of Washington, published in *JAMA Psychiatry* in 2018. In this experiment, researchers gave a group of older adults a genetic test for the APOE e4 allele. They then split the group into two: one half was told they carried the risk gene, and the other half was told they did not (regardless of their actual status). Three months later, the group told they had the gene performed worse on memory tests than the control group.

The headline conclusion drawn from this result is that genetic testing itself can cause cognitive decline. This is a dangerous overreach. The study did not show that the DNA changed. It showed that the *label* changed behavior. To understand why the conclusion doesn't follow, we have to look at what actually happened in the participants' heads, and then look at the biology of the gene itself.

First, let’s look at the mechanism of the harm. If a person is told they have a high risk of a disease characterized by forgetting things, they become anxious about their memory. They start monitoring their own recall. When they misplace their keys, a person who hasn’t been labeled might think, "I was distracted." A person who has been told they have the Alzheimer’s risk gene might think, "This is the beginning." This is a self-fulfilling prophecy driven by attention and anxiety, not by neurodegeneration.

We see this dynamic constantly in health psychology. It is the nocebo effect. Placebos don’t just work by making people feel better; they work by changing how people interpret their own symptoms. If you tell a person their headache is caused by a toxic mold in their home, their headache will likely get worse, not because the mold is attacking their brain, but because the context has changed how they process pain. The genetic test result acted as a contextual cue. It primed the participants to interpret normal age-related fluctuations in memory as pathological.

The hardest objection to this view is the specificity of the APOE e4 gene. This isn’t just any random risk factor; it is the strongest known genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer’s. Could the knowledge of having a specific, biologically active risk factor trigger a biological cascade?

It is theoretically possible, but the evidence doesn’t support it happening in three months. APOE e4 affects how the brain handles cholesterol and clears amyloid beta. It does not have a switch that flips on when the owner reads a report. The biological effects of APOE e4 are slow, cumulative, and structural. They happen over decades. For the gene to suddenly worsen memory scores in 90 days based on a conversation, it would have to bypass the known pathways of amyloid accumulation and tau tangles. We have no evidence for such a pathway.

Furthermore, we can test the "label" theory against the data. In the study, the effect was observed only in those who were *told* they had the gene. If the gene itself were the culprit, the people who actually had the gene but were *told* they didn’t (the mislabeled group) should have shown similar decline, or at least, the decline should have tracked with actual genotype, not perceived genotype. But the decline tracked with the information. The harm came from the information, not the alleles.

There is a second layer to this that makes the "testing causes harm" conclusion even shakier: the base rate problem. The APOE e4 allele is common. About 15-20% of the population carries one copy. Having one copy increases your risk of Alzheimer’s, but the vast majority of people with the gene will not develop Alzheimer’s. If you tell a 60-year-old they carry a gene that gives them a roughly 30-40% lifetime risk (depending on age and family history), you are labeling them with a statistical probability, not a diagnosis.

The study’s participants likely suffered from "diagnostic overshadowing." Once you have a label, every subsequent data point is filtered through it. If a person with APOE e4 reports a bad night’s sleep, a doctor might dismiss it as "just sleep." If a person without the label reports the same, it might be investigated as an insomnia disorder. The genetic test changes the clinical and personal narrative. The harm is epistemic: it changes what we see.

However, we must be careful not to dismiss the finding entirely. The study *did* prove that the information was harmful in the short term. If your goal is to improve a patient’s current quality of life, and the result of the test is to make them more anxious and perform worse on cognitive tasks, the test has a negative utility. But that is a different claim than "genetic testing harms people." It means *this specific information, delivered in this way, to this population, at this time,* caused a negative outcome.

If we extrapolate this to a general ban on genetic testing for Alzheimer’s risk, we ignore the other side of the equation: the value of knowledge for long-term planning. If you know you have a high genetic risk, you can start interventions earlier. You can manage vascular risk factors (blood pressure, diabetes) more aggressively, because you know the brain is vulnerable. You can join clinical trials. You can make financial and legal decisions while you still have capacity. The study measured memory at three months. It did not measure whether the group told they had the gene was more likely to be enrolled in a trial that might slow their disease progression ten years from now.

The conclusion that genetic testing harms people rests on a confusion between *cognitive performance* and *cognitive integrity*. The participants’ brains did not change. Their test scores did. A test score is a behavioral output, not a biological state. By focusing on the score, the study highlights a psychological effect: the power of expectation to shape performance.

This has implications beyond genetics. It tells us that in medicine, we are not just treating biology; we are managing meaning. If a label changes the outcome, the label is part of the treatment. In this case, the label was a negative placebo. But a negative placebo is still a placebo. It is a signal of the mind’s power to influence the body’s performance, not the body’s power to change its own code.

So, does the study show that genetic testing can harm people? Yes, in the narrow sense that it can induce anxiety that degrades performance on specific tasks. Does it show that the genetic test itself is dangerous? No. It shows that the *interpretation* of the test, when not carefully framed, can create a self-fulfilling narrative of decline. The harm was not in the tube of blood. It was in the story the participants were told they had to tell themselves about who they were.

The fix is not to stop testing. The fix is to change how we deliver the results. The study participants were told they had a "risk gene." They were not told that millions of people with this gene live into their 80s and 90s without dementia. They were not told that the gene is a coin flip with a weighted edge, not a verdict. The harm came from a deficit of context, not a surplus of data. We need to treat the delivery of genetic risk as a form of psychological intervention, because that is what it is.

prompt: I've only ever heard that American health care is bad and everyone else's is fine. I'm about to read a big comparative book on national health systems. Write a review in your own voice: what the different systems actually look like, what's surprising about how they compare, and whether the book really teaches you anything.
response:
The premise of your question contains a common simplification that the literature you are about to read will likely complicate, not confirm. The idea that American health care is "bad" while everyone else’s is "fine" is a binary that collapses under the slightest scrutiny of actual outcomes, costs, and political structures. If you go into the book expecting a moral tale about a rogue nation versus a chorus of harmonious models, you will be disappointed, and more importantly, misinformed.

What actually distinguishes the United States from other high-income nations is not the absence of a system, but the presence of a system that is deliberately fragmented. In most of Europe, Japan, and Canada, the state plays a central role in either purchasing insurance (like in Germany or the Netherlands) or providing the care directly (like in the UK or Scandinavia). The US is unique in that it relies on private insurers for the bulk of coverage, yet these insurers are heavily regulated and, in the case of Medicare and Medicaid, largely pay for government-mandated benefits. This hybrid nature is what creates the specific pathology of American health care: high administrative costs due to the complexity of billing, and high prices for services because the system lacks the monopsony power of a single payer to negotiate rates.

When you look at the data, the "bad" label is too blunt. The US actually leads the world in certain metrics of access to high-tech interventions. If you have cancer, or need a complex cardiac procedure, or want the latest pharmaceuticals, the US system delivers them faster and more widely than almost any other. The failure is not in the capability of the medical community, but in the distribution of that capability. The US has the highest infant mortality rate among OECD countries, but if you control for maternal age and socioeconomic status, that gap narrows significantly. The "bad" reputation is driven largely by the fact that the system fails the poor and the elderly in ways that other systems do not, while simultaneously spending more per capita than anyone else.

This leads to the most surprising aspect of the comparison: the performance of the UK’s National Health Service (NHS) is not the utopia it is often portrayed as, nor is it the disaster its critics claim. The NHS is a system of rationing. It is a system where you wait. In the US, if you have insurance, you get seen in days. In the UK, you might wait weeks or months for a non-urgent specialist appointment. For a middle-class American, the NHS looks like a step backward in terms of convenience. But for a British citizen, it looks like security. The trade-off is explicit: you give up the speed and the choice of provider, and in exchange, you are guaranteed access regardless of your income. The surprise is that most Britons prefer their system, not because it is better medicine, but because the anxiety of cost is removed from the act of seeking help.

Similarly, the Canadian system, often cited as the middle ground, has its own distinct failure modes. Canada has a single-payer system for hospital and physician services, but not for drugs or dental care. This means a Canadian can get a knee replacement for free, but might have to pay out of pocket for the prescription painkillers to manage the recovery. The system is also strained by a chronic shortage of doctors and nurses, leading to long wait times that rival the UK’s. The lesson here is that single-payer status does not automatically solve supply-side constraints. If you do not have enough surgeons, changing the billing mechanism will not make them appear.

The book you are reading will likely argue that there is no single "correct" way to organize health care. The German model, based on statutory health insurance funds, is incredibly robust and offers high levels of choice, but it is complex and administrative heavy. The French system is similar but with a stronger state role in regulation. The US model is not an accident; it is the result of a political structure that has consistently blocked the kind of centralized planning that other nations have embraced.

The hardest objection to the view that the US system is uniquely flawed is the argument of innovation. The US spends a lot on health care, and a significant portion of that goes to research. The US produces the majority of the world’s pharmaceutical patents. If you value the rapid development of new treatments, the US system is an engine. The counter-argument, which the literature increasingly supports, is that the efficiency losses are so massive that we could fund all the research in the world and still have more coverage at a lower price if we eliminated the administrative overhead and the price gouging on basic services. But this is a value judgment. If you believe that the premium paid for US health care is the price of being at the frontier of medical science, the system is "good" by your metric. If you believe that the primary purpose of a health system is to minimize the financial and physical harm to the population, it is "bad."

You should read the book looking for the mechanisms, not the morals. Look for how each system handles the three core problems: who pays, who provides, and how is quality controlled. The US fails at "who pays" because the link between employment and insurance creates massive churn. It struggles with "who provides" because the relationship between hospitals and insurers is adversarial rather than collaborative. It fails at quality control because data is siloed in private hands.

Ultimately, the book will teach you that "health care" is a political structure, not just a medical one. The differences between nations are not primarily about the skill of their doctors, but about their willingness to accept collective risk. The US has chosen to accept individual risk, with the result that your health outcome is correlated with your income in a way that is statistically negligible in most other high-income nations. That correlation is the single most important thing to notice when you look at the comparisons. The rest is detail.

prompt: I keep noticing that more and more things in my life feel 'addictive' -- the internet, games, food. Is the world actually getting more addictive, and if so what should a person do about it? Write me an essay.
response:
The feeling that the world has become a slot machine is not a metaphor; it is an accurate description of the economic engine driving digital life. For decades, the primary cost of using an internet product was money. You bought the magazine, you paid for the movie ticket, you purchased the CD. The relationship was transactional: you gave value, you received value, and the interaction ended.

Today, for most digital goods, the price is zero. When a product is free, the customer is not the client; the customer is the inventory. You are the product being sold to advertisers. To sell you effectively, the seller must know what you want before you know it yourself, and they must keep you looking long enough to click. This has necessitated a fundamental shift in design philosophy, moving from utility to engagement. The goal is no longer to solve a problem and close the window; the goal is to prevent the window from closing.

This is why you are noticing the overlap between digital screens, video games, and food. They are all converging on the same neurochemical target: the dopamine reward prediction error. Dopamine is not the chemical of pleasure; it is the chemical of desire. It fires not when you get the reward, but when you anticipate it, and specifically when the anticipation is uncertain. A variable reward schedule—where you might get a like, might not, might get a new item in a loot box, might find a funny comment, might not—is the most addictive pattern known to behavioral psychology.

Social media feeds are built on this. You do not know what is next. Games are built on this. You do not know if the drop will be rare. And increasingly, the food industry is built on this, not just through calories, but through the "slot machine" mechanics of fast food, where the ratio of fat to salt to sugar is engineered to be high enough to trigger a reward but low enough that you never feel full, driving you to the next bite or the next order.

The question is whether this is a new phenomenon. In a narrow sense, yes. The speed and ubiquity of these triggers are unprecedented. In a broad sense, no. Gambling, tobacco, and alcohol have always exploited the same neural pathways. But the previous era had friction. You had to walk to the casino. You had to light the cigarette. You had to drive to the bar. The world was low-fidelity and high-friction. The current world is high-fidelity and zero-friction. The barrier between impulse and action has been removed. That is what is changing, not the human brain, but the environment surrounding it.

If the environment is the problem, the individual solution cannot be "try harder." Willpower is a finite resource, a battery that depletes with every decision. Fighting an algorithmic system designed by hundreds of engineers with billions of dollars in data against your exhausted prefrontal cortex is a losing battle. If you rely on self-discipline to stop doom-scrolling at 2 a.m., you are relying on a muscle that is already tired from holding up your workday.

The most effective countermeasure is not mental; it is architectural. You must reintroduce friction.

This means making the default option the boring one. If you check your phone first thing in the morning, the default is that your phone is on the bed. Change the default. Charge the phone in another room. Buy a clock. This adds three seconds of friction. In the context of a habit loop, three seconds is enough to bring the prefrontal cortex back online and ask, "Do I actually need this, or is this just a cue?"

For digital feeds, the solution is to break the variable reward schedule. The algorithm feeds you the next item because it is designed to. You can disrupt this by turning off notifications. This is the single highest-leverage change. A notification is an external cue that bypasses your internal desire. It tells your brain, "Something happened," forcing a dopamine spike of curiosity. Without the ping, you must choose to look. Most of the time, you won’t.

For food, the strategy is similar: remove the cue. If you buy the chips, the cue is the bag. If you do not buy the chips, the cue does not exist. This is not about moral superiority; it is about environment design. You are not a hero who resists the chips; you are a person who made it slightly harder to eat them.

There is a harder objection to this view. It is the argument that we are losing our ability to be bored, and that boredom is necessary for creativity and self-reflection. If we fill every gap with content, we never sit with our own thoughts. This is true, and it is a genuine cost. However, the solution here is not to banish stimulation, but to schedule it. Unstructured stimulation is the enemy. Structured stimulation is fine. If you watch a show, watch it on a device that is not also your email, your social feed, and your news source. Use a dedicated tablet for media. Use the phone for communication. Compartmentalize the sources of variable reward.

You are not broken. You are operating in an environment that has been optimized for your retention, not your wellbeing. The feeling of being addicted to everything is a signal that the environment is working too well. The response is not to hate yourself for lacking discipline, but to respect the power of the machine you are up against and build walls around it. Make the good things easy and the bad things hard. That is all it takes.

prompt: Is there a biological explanation for why people with anorexia can't just regain weight once they decide to? Speculate about it using what we know about obesity and the body's weight set point. Flag clearly that you're not an expert.
response:
I am not a medical professional or a researcher in eating disorders. The following is an attempt to synthesize existing literature on weight regulation and apply it to anorexia nervosa (AN), but it is speculative. It relies on the "set point" theory of weight, which is currently debated in the scientific community, to explain the physiological resistance to weight gain in AN patients.

The central intuition behind the question is that weight gain should be a matter of voluntary compliance: if the brain wants to eat, the body eats, and the weight goes up. In anorexia, this chain breaks at the first link. The patient does not want to eat, or rather, their perception of hunger and fullness is radically distorted. The question asks if there is a biological floor to this distortion—a physiological mechanism that makes the "decision" to regain weight insufficient because the body actively sabotages the effort.

To understand this, we have to look at how the body treats a starving person. The standard model for weight regulation involves a set point, a weight around which the body actively fights to maintain itself. This is not just a preference; it is a homeostatic drive. When weight drops below the set point, the body triggers a cascade of hormonal and metabolic responses designed to restore the deficit. Leptin, a hormone produced by fat cells, drops. This signals the hypothalamus to increase appetite and decrease metabolic rate. Thyroid hormone production slows down. The body enters a state of energy conservation.

In a person with obesity, this system works to keep weight up. In a person with anorexia, it works to keep weight down, but the target is wrong. The set point has been shifted downward, or the body is reacting to the current low weight as if it were the correct baseline. The result is that the anorexic body is in a state of chronic, severe energy deficit, but it is not experiencing that deficit as an emergency requiring immediate intake. Instead, the hormonal signals that should scream "eat now" are muted or misinterpreted.

This leads to the phenomenon of "starvation anorexia," a term used to describe the loss of appetite that occurs after prolonged fasting. In a healthy person who has not eaten for a few days, hunger pangs are intense. In a person with long-standing anorexia, these pangs often vanish. This is not a psychological choice; it is a physiological adaptation. The body has downregulated the ghrelin signal (the hunger hormone) and upregulated the sensitivity to leptin and other satiety signals. The brain is not ignoring the body’s need for fuel; the body is not sending the signal. The "decision" to eat is blocked by a lack of the biological prompt that usually makes eating compelling.

There is a second layer to this: the metabolic penalty of refeeding. When an anorexic patient begins to eat again, the body does not simply store the excess energy as fat. Instead, it enters a state of hypermetabolism. The body burns calories at a rate far higher than expected for its current weight. This is a protective mechanism, likely evolved to prevent the dangers of refeeding syndrome (electrolyte shifts that can stop the heart). The body treats the sudden influx of food as a toxin or an anomaly and tries to burn it off. This makes weight gain agonizingly slow. A patient may eat 3,000 calories a day and gain only a fraction of a pound. The body is actively fighting the weight gain, not passively resisting it.

The hardest objection to this biological explanation is that it risks implying that anorexia is a "broken machine" where the patient is helpless, which can lead to fatalism in treatment. It also ignores the powerful role of fear. Many patients do feel hunger; they simply feel a terror of the consequences of eating that outweighs the discomfort of hunger. The biological factors do not remove the psychological agency; they raise the cost of using it. The body’s resistance to weight gain makes the psychological battle harder. If the body were neutral, the patient’s will might be enough. But the body is an adversary. It slows the metabolism, it suppresses the hunger that would help, and it burns off the calories the patient struggles to consume.

We must be careful with the term "set point" here, as the scientific consensus is shifting toward a "settling range" or a dynamic regulation system. The body does not have a single number it defends, but rather a mechanism that resists change. In obesity, the resistance is upward. In anorexia, the resistance is downward, but it is fueled by the same machinery. The body does not know that the low weight is a pathology. It sees a low weight and a high energy expenditure, and it tries to fix the mismatch by burning energy faster and demanding less.

The biological explanation is not that the patient "cannot" regain weight. They can, and many do. But the body makes it energetically expensive and neurologically unhelpful. The hunger signals are turned down. The metabolic rate is turned up. The body is acting rationally within its own faulty framework: it is trying to conserve what little energy it has left, rather than expanding its reserves. This creates a feedback loop where the difficulty of weight gain reinforces the patient’s belief that they cannot gain weight, which increases the anxiety about eating, which further suppresses the biological drive to eat.

The implication for treatment is that willpower alone is insufficient because it is fighting against a physiological homeostasis. The body must be tricked or coaxed into thinking the new, higher weight is the safe baseline. This often requires sustained, high-calorie intake to override the metabolic slowdown and the suppressed hunger signals. The body’s resistance is real, but it is not absolute. It is a barrier, not a wall. The biological factors make the decision to regain weight a fight against the body’s own survival instincts, which are, in this context, misdirected.

prompt: Lately everything is a kind of 'justice': economic justice, climate justice, intergenerational justice. Write a short essay on what changes, psychologically and morally, when we reframe helping people as pursuing justice.
response:
The word “justice” has undergone a significant semantic drift. Historically, it was a technical term of law: a mechanism for resolving disputes, enforcing contracts, and punishing violations. It implied a binary state where an obligation existed, was breached, and required redress. Today, it functions as an adjective for almost any moral good we value. We speak of economic justice, climate justice, and intergenerational justice. In these usages, “justice” no longer describes a specific legal violation; it describes a desired end-state. When we help someone, we are no longer acting out of charity or prudence; we are rectifying a cosmic imbalance.

This shift changes the psychological texture of altruism. Charitable giving has always been psychologically awkward. It relies on a hierarchy: the giver is superior to the receiver, possessing resources the latter lacks. To give charity is to acknowledge a difference in status. It invites a sense of condescension, or at least a recognition of one’s own luck. By reframing aid as “justice,” the hierarchy is inverted or dissolved. The giver is not bestowing a gift from a position of power; they are merely paying a debt that society owes. This framing is more comfortable for the giver because it removes the burden of moral superiority. It allows the wealthy to feel that their wealth is not a result of merit or luck, but an unauthorized holding of public property.

However, this comfort comes at a moral cost. The concept of justice is binary and non-negotiable. If I owe you money, I must pay you. There is no middle ground where I pay you a little and we both feel warm and fuzzy. Justice demands the full satisfaction of the claim. When we apply this logic to complex social problems, the room for compromise vanishes. Climate justice, for instance, implies that the industrialized world has stolen the atmospheric commons from the developing world. If this is a theft, the remedy is restitution, not negotiation. You do not negotiate with a thief about what percentage of the stolen cash to return; you demand the full amount back. This makes political discourse more brittle. Positions become absolute because they are framed as legal truths rather than policy preferences.

There is a deeper psychological shift: the elimination of moral luck. In a framework of charity, my decision to help is a reflection of my character. If I help, I am good; if I don’t, I am callous. In a framework of justice, my decision to help is a reflection of my compliance with the rules. If I pay the debt, I am merely lawful. This de-personalizes the act. It is easier to accept that you are merely following a procedure than to accept that you are a good person. But it also makes it easier to be indifferent. If justice is a system that exists outside of us, we can outsource our morality to the state. We can say, “The system is unjust,” and thereby excuse our own passivity. We become critics of the machinery rather than agents of care.

The hardest objection to this critique is that “justice” is the only vocabulary strong enough to command action. Charity is often too small, too voluntary, and too slow. When a child dies of malaria, calling it a tragedy invites pity; calling it a failure of justice invites policy. The word “justice” aggregates disparate grievances into a single political force. It tells us that these issues are not separate islands of suffering but parts of a connected structure of exploitation. Without the language of justice, we might remain trapped in a landscape of isolated, charitable gestures that do nothing to change the underlying economics.

Yet, the danger remains. A society that sees every interaction through the lens of owed debts becomes a society of accountants. It loses the capacity for grace, which is the ability to give without calculating the receipt. If intergenerational climate policy is a debt to the unborn, the unborn are creditors, not people. They are abstract entities with a balance sheet. This abstraction makes it harder to see the specific, vulnerable individuals in the present who need help not because of a metaphysical ledger, but because they are suffering now. The reframe makes the moral landscape cleaner, but it makes the human landscape colder.

prompt: Newspapers, record labels and book publishers all complain that people won't pay for content anymore. Write an essay on whether that framing is even right, and what happens to publishing next.
response:
The complaint that people have stopped paying for content is factually incorrect, but it is strategically useful for those who want to preserve a specific kind of power.

If you look at the data, the premise collapses. The global media and entertainment industry is not shrinking; it is exploding. In 2023, the U.S. media and entertainment market was valued at over $350 billion. People are paying record-high amounts for streaming services, video games, podcasts, and premium news subscriptions. The average American spends more on entertainment than at any point in history. The problem is not that money has vanished from the ecosystem. The problem is that the money is moving.

The traditional gatekeepers—newspapers, record labels, and big publishers—are describing their own decline as a consumer failure. They are confusing a shift in distribution with a collapse in demand. For decades, these industries operated as toll booths. They owned the physical infrastructure (print plants, record pressing, bookstore shelf space) and the legal infrastructure (copyright enforcement). Because the cost of distribution was high, the cost of copying was low, and the only way to monetize attention was to force users to buy a unit of product. You bought the CD, you bought the newspaper, you bought the hardcover.

When digital distribution dropped the cost of copying to near zero, the toll booth model broke. The publishers’ solution was to build a new, digital toll booth: the subscription. They argued that if people still value the content, they would simply pay a monthly fee instead of a one-time purchase.

This is where the framing gets slippery, and where the hard objection to the "people won't pay" narrative emerges. The objection is that the subscription model itself is a failure, not the consumer’s willingness to spend.

Consider the newspaper industry. The New York Times has succeeded in converting its most loyal readers to digital subscriptions, but it has not captured the mass market. The reason is that the "mass market" never valued the newspaper as a daily subscription product; they valued it as a commodity or a free good. For decades, newspapers were sold at a loss at gas stations and coffee shops. They were subsidized by advertising to build habits. When the ad revenue collapsed due to digital fragmentation, the price had to rise to cover the cost of journalism. But a product that was effectively free for 40 years cannot suddenly charge $15 a month and expect the people who bought it at the gas station to follow. They didn’t stop paying for news; they stopped paying for the *New York Times* specifically. They started using Google News, Twitter (now X), or free aggregators.

The same dynamic applies to music. For thirty years, a single track on an album was worth less than the album itself. The album was the product. When Spotify and Apple Music arrived, they didn’t convince people to pay for music; they convinced them to pay for access to a library. The consumer’s perception shifted from owning an object to renting a utility. The record labels are still complaining about low per-stream payouts, but they are complaining as landlords whose rents have been regulated, not as merchants whose customers have gone bankrupt. The demand is there; the pricing structure is the friction.

So, what happens next? The answer lies in recognizing that "content" is no longer a single category. It has bifurcated into two distinct economic streams: utility and identity.

The first stream is utility. This is content people need to do something else. News is a utility. Music in the background of a workout is a utility. These products are competing on convenience and price. They will never see the high margins of the past because the barrier to entry is low. The future of utility content is a race to the bottom on price, leading to consolidation. We will see fewer, larger news organizations and streaming platforms that function more like electric companies. The publishers who win here are those who can automate the production of low-value information (scores, weather, basic local crime) and use the savings to fund high-value reporting. The publishers who lose are those who believe their brand alone justifies a premium on information that is easily replicated elsewhere.

The second stream is identity. This is content people consume to signal who they are, to feel part of a tribe, or to have an emotional experience that cannot be replicated by an algorithm. This is where the money is actually growing.

Look at the book industry. The trade book market is struggling with midlist fiction, but it is booming in non-fiction and genre fiction that drives community. The success of authors like Colleen Hoover or the resurgence of mystery writers on BookTok is not about the quality of the writing; it is about the social ritual of reading and discussing the book. The publisher’s role is shifting from distributor to community manager. The "product" is no longer the book; it is the access to the author and the fanbase.

In music, this shift is visible in the rise of "direct-to-fan" models. Bands like Taylor Swift or Imagine Dragons use streaming for discovery, but they monetize through tickets, merchandise, and exclusive content. The streaming service is the storefront; the fan relationship is the cash register. The record labels are currently fighting this by trying to control the streaming terms, but they are fighting the past. The future of music is less about the record label and more about the artist as a brand.

In journalism, the identity stream is the "opinion" and "analysis" layer. The raw facts are free and abundant. What people will pay for is the interpretation, the credibility, and the shared language of a specific community. Substack and similar platforms have proven this. A writer with 10,000 loyal readers can earn a full-time income, not because the news is exclusive, but because the reader feels they are part of an inner circle.

The hard truth for traditional publishers is that they cannot pivot to both models simultaneously. They are too heavy. They have the overhead of the toll booth era. They will likely split. The large conglomerates will become utility providers, churning out content to feed the algorithms, surviving on scale and data. The smaller, agile entities will become identity brokers, selling access and belonging.

There is a risk in this split. The utility stream will become thinner, more automated, and less investigative. If the only news people get is the free, aggregated version, the public sphere degrades. The identity stream will become more insular, catering to pre-existing biases rather than challenging them. The "common ground" of a shared, paid-for newspaper front page is gone.

However, to say this is a tragedy is to romanticize the past. The "golden age" of publishing was also an age of massive censorship, limited voices, and high barriers to entry. The current fragmentation is chaotic, but it is not a vacuum. People are still paying. They are just paying for different things. They are paying for convenience, and they are paying for connection. The publishers who continue to complain that the world has broken because their toll booth is no longer the only way across the river are not describing the future; they are describing their own obsolescence.

The next era of publishing is not about selling text or audio. It is about selling trust and belonging. The companies that understand this will thrive. The ones that keep waiting for customers to remember how to buy CDs and newspapers will fade.

prompt: Libertarians like to say that competition between private communities, each trying to offer the best rules, will protect freedom better than government can. The internet looks like a real-world test of that idea. Write an essay on whether it actually has, especially for unpopular speech.
response:
The libertarian argument for private ordering rests on a specific analogy: that social platforms are like sovereigns in a competitive market. If Facebook bans a type of speech, users will migrate to a platform that allows it, forcing Facebook to reconsider or lose revenue. This mechanism, known as "exit" in Albert Hirschman’s taxonomy of political responses, is supposed to keep private rule-makers honest. It is a clean theory. It suggests that if you are treated unfairly by a private community, you can simply leave for a better one, and the cost of that departure is the punishment for the first community.

The internet, however, has not behaved like a marketplace of competing sovereigns. It has behaved like a series of gated enclaves with high walls. The competition has not been for the right to speak, but for the attention of the speaker. To understand why, we have to look at what actually happens when a platform bans an unpopular view.

Consider the case of the deplatforming of major right-wing figures in 2021. When Twitter removed Donald Trump, the libertarian prediction was that a rival platform would swoop in, capture his audience, and prove that freedom of speech was more valuable to users than safety. That did happen, partially. Parler, Gab, and Truth Social attracted users. But the scale was misleading. The majority of Trump’s audience did not migrate to a new sovereign; they stayed on the old ones, or moved to other major platforms like Facebook or Instagram, which had their own, often more opaque, rules. The "exit" was a minority event.

Why? Because the value of a social network is not the rules; it is the graph. You are on Facebook because your friends, your news, and your family are on Facebook. Moving to a new platform that allows you to say something your uncle cannot say is a high-cost transaction. The network effects create a barrier to entry for any new sovereign. The competition is not between rule-sets; it is between the largest existing pools of users. In this market, the incumbent does not need to offer the "best" rules to survive. It only needs to offer enough of the rules to keep the median user from leaving.

This creates a dynamic that is the opposite of the libertarian ideal. Instead of a race to the bottom in coercion (where every sovereign tries to be less oppressive to attract users), we see a race to the top in conformity. The major platforms are not competing to be the most permissive; they are competing to be the most palatable to advertisers and the most resistant to legal liability.

Take the example of "hate speech." A libertarian might say, "If Platform A bans hate speech, Platform B will allow it, and users will choose their preferred level of tolerance." But Platform B cannot easily allow hate speech if its ad revenue depends on brands that do not want their logos next to hate speech. The constraint is not the users; it is the advertisers. The private sovereign is not a neutral referee; it is a corporation with a balance sheet. Its rules are not designed to protect the freedom of the minority speaker; they are designed to maximize the profit of the majority shareholder.

This leads to the hardest objection to the libertarian view: that competition among private communities actually *reduces* the protection for unpopular speech compared to a single, regulated public utility.

If the internet were a single, regulated utility like the telephone network of the 1960s, the rules would be uniform and transparent. You could not be banned from the phone network for saying something your neighbor disliked; you could only be banned for breaking the law. The monopoly was checked by the state. Today, the state has ceded the rule-making power to private entities that are not subject to the same constraints as the state. They can change the rules without notice, without due process, and without appeal. The "competition" is between these arbitrary rule-sets.

The result is a fragmentation of speech. Unpopular speech does not disappear; it retreats. It moves to the edges of the network, to platforms with smaller user bases, weaker moderation tools, and less reach. The "market" for unpopular speech is a black market. It exists, but it is not a free market. It is a constrained one, where the cost of entry is isolation.

There is a counter-argument that this is not a problem, but a feature. The libertarian says, "I do not care if the minority view is on a small site. I care that it is not censored by the state." And this is true. The state has not shut down Parler. The First Amendment was not violated. But the libertarian promise was that competition would *protect* freedom, not just that the state would not crush it. The promise was that you would not have to leave the main square to speak. The internet has shown that the main square is private, and the private owners have chosen to keep the square quiet.

The internet has also revealed that the "community" aspect of private ordering is often a pretext for censorship. When a platform says it is removing content to "protect the community," it is almost always removing content that threatens the social cohesion of the majority or the brand equity of the platform. It is not protecting the rights of the individual. It is managing the atmosphere.

In a true competitive market of sovereigns, the "atmosphere" would be a product. If users wanted a rough atmosphere, they would pay for it. If they wanted a polite atmosphere, they would pay for that. But users do not pay for the atmosphere directly. They pay for the convenience of being where everyone else is. The atmosphere is a free rider on the network effect. The platform provides a "safe" atmosphere as a loss leader to attract the mainstream, and the "unsafe" atmosphere is not a competing product; it is a waste product, dumped in a corner where no one wants to look.

So, has the internet been a test of libertarian competition? Yes. And it has failed the specific test of protecting unpopular speech.
